#6767. Why Peptide Skincare Might Actually Be Worth Your While, According to Experts

The recent buzz around peptides came to a head last month when U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced that six unregulated injectables, including the highly controversial “Wolverine stack” BPC-157 and TB-500, will now be available for broad use throughout the United States. Meanwhile, unsurprising to derms and estheticians everywhere, the rising tide of interest in peptides has spilled over into skincare, where the molecules have long served as an active ingredient.

“I’ve had a lot of patients come in since the HHS ruling,” says Erik Peterson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City, who likens the recent policy change to “opening the floodgates,” resulting in a surge of interest—particularly from patients who’ve come across claims of peptide-based skincare being like ‘botox in a bottle.’

“It’s interesting how they are suddenly so popular, because peptides have been around for like 30 years in skincare,” says Malika Sloan, medical esthetician and founder of Sloan Studio in New York City. “They’ve been incorporated into cosmetic formulations for decades, with ingredients like matrixyl helping to popularize them in the early 2000s. What’s exciting now is how much more sophisticated the formulations have become.”

If you’re curious about peptide-based skincare products—what they potentially can do, what they definitely cannot—and which products experts recommend for the best results, here’s everything you need to know.

Peptides, regardless of whether they’re injected via syringe or applied topically with a serum or cream, are short chains of amino acids that instruct your body to execute specific functions. Insulin, for example, is a peptide that helps the body regulate blood sugar, and it’s been in use since the 1920s. More recently, GLP-1 drugs (short for glucagon-like peptide-1) have been found to curb food cravings and slow stomach emptying, making them highly effective for weight loss. The list of uses for peptides is virtually endless, ranging from muscle growth and wound healing to balancing hormones and managing inflammation.

In skincare, topical peptides work much the same way as their injectable counterparts, but on a more localized level, directing your skin to carry out specific functions, “the first of which tends to be increasing production of collagen and elastin, which are two of the major determinants of skin quality,” says Dr. Peterson. They’ve also been shown to help even out skin tone, repair the skin barrier, and reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles.

The world of peptides is still a bit of a Wild West. A quick Google search for peptide skincare will yield dozens of results for unresearched compounds promising you flawless skin. And then, of course, there are the influencers. “You see all these kids on TikTok who are talking about their beauty routines, and they’re like 19 years old,” says Peterson. “It’s like, ‘Amazing, your skin obviously looks great, because you’re a child.’” In reality, the list of peptides that you can truly depend on to move the needle (without an actual needle) is surprisingly short, at least until more research is done.

“The two peptides that are out right now that have any sort of viable data on them are palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 and GHK-Cu,” says Peterson. Signaling peptides, as they’re called—such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, better known as matrixyl—have some of the strongest clinical and anecdotal evidence for stimulating collagen and reducing the appearance of wrinkles. Although, as Peterson points out, much of the scientific data has been industry funded, “so we always have to be a bit skeptical.”

Carrier peptides—like GHK-Cu, a popular copper peptide—on the other hand, “have some good lab data, but very minimal human data,” Peterson says. Nonetheless, products containing GHK-Cu are widely heralded for their ability to repair damaged tissue, reduce inflammation, and stimulate production of collagen and elastin. “I find copper peptides particularly interesting because of the research surrounding tissue repair and collagen-related remodeling pathways,” says Sloan.

As for acetyl hexapeptide-8, or argireline, as it’s more commonly known—aka “botox in a bottle”—don’t waste your money. “From a physiological perspective, it can’t possibly work,” says Peterson, who explains that the molecules of this particular peptide are simply too large to pass through the surface of the skin. He compares it to skincare products that contain collagen rather than spur the body to produce its own. “Collagen is a massive molecule,” he says. “It would be like putting cow’s milk on your face—it’s not going to do anything.” Sure enough, a 2023 study found the effects of topical argireline to be “not statistically significant.”

Instead, for those looking for the most noticeable results, Sloan recommends seeking out products that combine proven peptides with complementary, similarly validated ingredients—like SkinCeuticals’ P-TIOX Anti-Wrinkle Peptide Cream. “I like that the cream also incorporates ceramides, niacinamide, and moisturizing ingredients, making it an interesting option for someone looking to address both hydration and visible signs of aging,” she says. Peterson’s pick, The Rich Cream from Augustinus Bader, flanks signaling peptides with hyaluronic acid and vitamin E to improve moisture retention and bolster the skin’s protective barrier.

Peptides are a relatively low-maintenance addition to most skin regimens. “One of the reasons I love incorporating peptides into at-home skincare is that they’re generally well tolerated and relatively easy to combine with other ingredients,” says Sloan, who notes that peptides can typically be used alongside other popular actives like vitamin C, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, and retinoids. “I typically recommend incorporating a peptide serum after cleansing and before moisturizer,” she says.

Just keep in mind that peptides alone won’t take the place of a well-rounded skincare regimen. “The best, most robust data still comes from the tried-and-true favorites of all dermatologists—protecting your collagen with consistent sunscreen use, and the best signaling molecule of them all: topical retinoids,” Peterson says.

And, of course, don’t expect overnight results—despite what social media might have you believe. “Peptides are just signals for your skin, not magic in a bottle,” Peterson says. “The few studies that there are show at least three months of consistent usage before results are seen, so stick it out if you want to give it a real try.”

#6766. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6765. Gloria Steinem’s Memorial Was a Celebration—and One Big Talking Circle

“Celebrating the glorious life of Gloria.” Those were the words projected against a red backdrop behind the stage at the Park Avenue Armory on Wednesday evening. Politicians (some, like Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan, newly elected in the midterm Democratic sweep), performers, and poets gathered alongside Gloria Steinem’s family and chosen family to memorialize the pioneering activist, who died in September at 92 years old.

The mood was celebratory, which is, according to her friends who organized the occasion, exactly what she wanted. That, and no mentions of God, said fellow activist and author Amy Richards, drawing a laugh from the crowd.

Former first ladies Michelle Obama and Jill Biden were among those front and center, with Meg Ryan, Marisa Tomei, Bette Midler, Diane von Furstenberg, Ashley Judd, Thelma Golden, Lucy Liu, Keri Russell, Candice Bergen, Annie Leibovitz, Anita Hill, Christy Turlington, and Padma Lakshmi. Attendees sat in chairs arranged in giant semi-circles to mirror the talking circles Steinem regularly hosted at her Upper East Side apartment (the final one took place with a group of teenagers just three weeks before her death). The guest list reflected Steinem’s wide-ranging reach. “There’s nothing intimidating about this room at all,” quipped producer and philanthropist Abigail Disney.

The night kicked off with the song “Hold On” by Heidi Wilson, which was written in 2018 after the suicide of a Vermont teenager and went on to be adopted as an anthem of solidarity during more recent protests in Minneapolis and New York. It was performed by a group dubbed ‘Gloria’s Choir,’ which included the Indigo Girls, actress Emma Watson, Leona Naess, and the members of indie rock band Betty, who have been together since 1986. “Gloria was our favorite rockstar,” said Betty bassist Alyson Palmer, beaming.

Alice Walker, one of Steinem’s closest friends, couldn’t be there, so Mariska Hargitay took to the stage to read “She,” a poem Walker wrote for Steinem on her 75th birthday: “She is the one whowithout hesitation comes to my aid and my defense. / She is the one who believes my side of the story first. / She is the one whose heart is open. / She is our sister, our teacher, our friend.”

Barbara Lee, the first Black woman mayor of Oakland and Steinem’s friend and collaborator of over 50 years, spoke passionately about their early activist years with Bella Abzug and campaigning for Shirley Chisholm. “When others stepped away, Gloria stepped forward,” she said.

“Hello everybody, I’m Marlo,” said a glowing Marlo Thomas as she adjusted the mic, as if anyone needed an introduction. It was during her time playing the single, struggling actress Ann Marie on That Girl that she first crossed paths with Steinem. Thomas was approached about playing Steinem on screen and in a meeting for the project the would-be producer looked at the two of them and said, “I don’t know which one of you I want to f*ck first.” The meeting was a bust, of course, Thomas said, but their friendship endured and the two spent countless holidays together. Thomas was at Steinem’s bedside during her final days, reading Native American prayers and Googling the Kaddish so she could recite it to her.

Musician Blake Morgan read a poem by his mother Robin Morgan, the poet, activist, and editor of the seminal feminist anthology Sisterhood Is Powerful, who died a few days after Steinem. Morgan and Steinem, along with three other women, had met monthly for dinner for the past 50 years, and their enduring friendship inspired the words of the poem “Giants at the Corner Table.” “There will be three someday, then two, then one. / That one will carry in herself some of the best of all of us because in each other’s presence some of the best of each of us came forth. / And when she goes, the women we were to one another will all wink out, the work we’ve shared lasting perhaps a little while beyond us.”

Cyndi Lauper, in leather pants and pink-streaked hair, declared that “without Gloria, there wouldn’t have been ‘Girls Just Wanna Have Fun,’” before launching into an acoustic rendition of her most famous song. Obama was the first one in the crowd to stand up and start dancing and singing along, prompting everyone to follow her lead.

Chelsea Handler brought laughs—even without ribbing men—and Amanda Gorman gave a captivating recitation of her poem “We Rise.” Cynthia Erivo was initially slated to sing “I Won’t Complain,” but changed course after hearing the speeches to perform “Imagine” instead. “Gloria imagined possibility,” she said, before giving an electrifying rendition of the John Lennon classic that reflected the night’s message of hope: every attendee was asked to wear a button that said “Hope-aholic.”

Public-interest lawyer, social justice activist, and founder of the Equal Justice Initiative Bryan Stevenson delivered what might have been the night’s most impassioned tribute to Steinem, using anecdotes from his own upbringing and their longstanding friendship to highlight her feminist and anti-racism stance. “Is there a woman who made you?” he recalled Steinem asking him after he shared a story with her about when he first declared himself a feminist. His grandmother, he said—the daughter of people enslaved in Virginia and his family’s lodestar, who would also live into her nineties, and whom he could still feel hugging him in moments of conflict and challenge. Stevenson said Steinem, like his grandmother, always moved with love, ending with a powerful message that left the audience in tears: “To be free is to do what’s right, and Gloria died a free woman, which is rare, because of how she lived her life.”

Former senator Hillary Rodham Clinton, with her daughter Chelsea looking on, gave a closing speech that highlighted Steinem’s love of Louisa May Alcott (an image of Little Women hung behind the stage along with other banners that read “Smash the Patriarchy” and “It’s Steinemite!”). Clinton spoke about her admiration for Steinem, which started when she was in college at the height of the women’s movement, and how Steinem’s work paved a path for her own political career. “She helped make it possible for someone like me to run for president, to win a major party nomination and the popular vote… in case you forgot,” Clinton said, smiling, bringing an uproarious crowd to its feet. Clinton held a torch aloft in her hands as she echoed Steinem’s mission of passing it on to others. “Gloria gave us 92 years of light,” Clinton said, “and all the tools, memories, inspiration, and hope that we need to keep that light burning.”

The celebration ended as an all-out party as Kathy Sledge took to the stage, backed by Gloria’s Choir and Lauper, to belt out “We Are Family.” A solemn memorial service, this was not. The audience sang, clapped, danced, and joyfully waved their hands in unison. Fogo Azul, a New York-based reggae samba drum line of women, transgender, and nonbinary percussionists, appeared to ecstatically escort the crowd out of the massive room. It turns out that the timing of this week’s event was fortuitous: It fell on what would have been the birthday of Steinem’s friend, the late Native American activist Wilma Mankiller (who also wrote the lyrics for one of the night’s musical tributes, an art song for voice and string quartet in the Cherokee language by composer Anjelica Lindsey called “I Want to Be Reincarnated as Gloria Steinem”) and days before a memorial honoring labor leader Dolores Huerta.

Almost everyone who took the stage spoke about the importance not just of preserving Steinem’s memory, but of continuing her work; of carrying on her activism and organizing; of not retreating from her commitment to equality and justice; of why it was necessary to “keep on keeping on,” as Bryan Stevenson phrased it.

“We will not let her work end without her physical presence,” Barbara Lee said. Gloria’s Foundation is already proof of that. The organization continues to raise money to carry on her mission and even preserve her apartment as a refuge for women’s activism and gathering in perpetuity. Steinem may be gone, but this week made clear that her spirit is still very much alive and in capable hands. As Mariska Hargitay said from the stage, “Gloria will always exist in the present tense.”

#6764. Pumpkin Chiffon Pie

Classic pumpkin pie may be the most well-known pumpkin pie come the holidays, but let us make our case for its underappreciated, fancy cousin: Pumpkin Chiffon Pie. Impossibly light and fluffy, the filling is made by folding meringue into a pumpkin curd-esque mixture for a slice that truly is light as a feather. With this at your Thanksgiving table, we doubt anyone would miss the classic.

What People Are Saying:“Best Pumpkin Chiffon! I have tried multiple recipes and this one was easy and delicious! My husband loved it! Thanks so much! Merry Christmas!” - PurpleWheel

Before making the filling, we need to make and bake our pie crust. Start by preheating the oven to 375° and lightly greasing a 9” pie dish with cooking spray.

On a clean, lightly floured surface, roll out your pie dough into a 12” circle of even thickness. Carefully drape it over the prepared pie dish and gently press it into the bottom and edges, taking care not to stretch the dough and create weak points. Prick the bottom of the dough with a fork to prevent bubbling while baking, then trim any excess dough from the edges so you have about 1” of overhang. Tuck the overhang under itself and crimp the edges. Then, place the dough into the fridge to chill for 30 minutes (or, if you’re in a rush, into the freezer for 10 minutes).

Remove the chilled crust from the refrigerator and line it with parchment paper. Fill the pie dish with dried beans or pie weights and place it into the oven to blind bake for about 18 to 20 minutes. Once the edges are lightly golden, remove the parchment and weights and bake for 5 to 10 minutes more, until fully golden and cooked through. Remove the crust from the oven and place it in the fridge to cool for at least 2 hours.

Once the crust has chilled completely, place a medium saucepan on the stove and whisk together ½ cup sugar with the gelatin, pumpkin pie spice, and salt.

Then, in a medium bowl, whisk together the pumpkin puree, egg yolks, and milk until smooth, then pour the mixture into the saucepan with the sugar and gelatin mixture and whisk to combine.

Turn the burner under the saucepan on to medium heat and stir constantly until the mixture is hot and small bubbles are beginning to form around the edges. Remove the saucepan from the heat and transfer the mixture to a large bowl to cool to room temperature.

In a separate bowl, use a hand mixer to beat together the egg whites and cream of tartar until soft peaks form. Then, add the remaining ¼ cup sugar, one tablespoon at a time, continuing to beat until stiff peaks form.

Transfer ¼ of the whipped egg whites into the cooled pumpkin mixture and gently fold to combine. Then add the remaining egg whites and fold to combine again. Pour the mixture into the cooled pie crust and smooth the top before placing it into the refrigerator for at least 4 hours and up to overnight. Once it has cooled and set completely, top the pie with whipped cream and a sprinkle of pumpkin spice before slicing and serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found below.

A chiffon is typically made with a filling (often containing gelatin, like in this recipe) that's usually cooked over a double boiler before whipped cream gets folded in for a luxurious texture. The whole thing is poured into a pre-baked (like in this recipe) or no-bake crust and refrigerated.

If you want to save time (and counter space) by making your Thanksgiving dishes ahead of time, this is the pie for you. The entire pie requires chilling for at least four hours, up to overnight before serving, so you can easily make this the day before, then simply top with whipped cream when you're ready to serve. Leftovers can be stored covered in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.

#6763. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6762. Exclusive: Shohei Ohtani Just Signed a Historic Deal With New Balance

Shohei Ohtani is used to making history. In addition to his four MLB MVP awards and two World Series rings, the Los Angeles Dodgers two-way great is the first member of the 50/50 club (having racked up 54 home runs and 59 stolen bases during the 2024 season), became the first player to hit three homers and record 10 strikeouts in a single game (which he managed in a 2025 NLCS contest against the Brewers), and earlier this year maintained simultaneous streaks in games on base (48) and innings without an earned run (32 and two-thirds).

Now, the 32-year-old Japanese icon is adding to those accolades with a pioneering endorsement deal, officially extending his relationship with his longtime partner New Balance through to the end of his baseball career. (While a rarefied group of athletes have signed lifetime sponsorship deals—including LeBron James and Cristiano Ronaldo at Nike, and Damian Lillard at Adidas—Ohtani’s new contract appears to be both the first to exclusively cover a star’s playing days and the first of its kind in MLB.)

“There’s a lot of trust,” Ohtani tells me through an interpreter during a sit-down in Boston of his decision to commit to the New England sportswear stalwart for the long haul. “We’ve obviously built friendships, as well. They’ve been able to accommodate my requests, the things I’ve asked for, and, like I said, that takes the involvement of a lot of trust. That relationship has been very, very good and smooth. I had no reservations about extending our relationship.”

Earlier in the day, I shadowed Ohtani at New Balance’s headquarters, where, as part of the agreement, the company is renaming its on-site think tank as the Shohei Ohtani Sports Research Lab. A team of specialists led the Dodgers superstar through a slew of shoes—including his on-field Ohtani 1 model, which will receive new editions in 2027—and then a rack of branded apparel. All of it falls under his Shohei Ohtani Signature Collection, which New Balance launched in 2024 (about a year and a half after the athlete first signed with the company). The collection has grown deliberately and unhurriedly ever since—mirroring his patience in the batter’s box; Ohtani is methodical when it comes to product development and uninterested in rolling out rushed goods with his name slapped on them.

While conducting a kind of footwear postmortem on his 2026 season—which started well, but ended with a rare slump (and left knee and right biceps injuries that kept him from pitching after July 3)—Ohtani noted there’d been some moments of slippage on the heel of his landing foot when pitching. On a printed-out diagram, he used a pencil to sketch ways in which the shoe’s spikes might be slightly reconfigured to find a sweet spot for stability on the mound and speed around the bases. The question of switching footwear between pitching and batting comes up, but Ohtani has not yet done this (and it seems the consensus is to stick with one shoe only).

“I have a lot of direct input into the footwear and apparel,” Ohtani says. “That includes my style, which I like to keep simple, as well as performance-based requests, [like with my] spikes. Some years we make minor changes, and sometimes we’ll make a big change. They understand what I want.”

Ohtani’s apparel line runs across three categories: performance, lifestyle, and fanwear. His custom logo—a striking ink drawing of his figure, designed by the Japanese manga artist Takehiko Inoue—is featured subtly on the bulk of the lineup. “Shohei doesn’t see himself as a glamorous player,” Chris Davis, New Balance brand president and chief marketing officer, tells me. “He sees himself as a gritty, hardworking athlete who wants to get better every day, and his logo reflects this—it has this kind of quiet intensity.”

While some of the future apparel designs boast cool technical features—like detachable, two-in-one, and reversible elements inspired by Ohtani’s two-way play—the man himself is only concerned that his products “fit comfortably and to be easy to wear.” When asked if there’s anyone whose style he likes or is influenced by, Ohtani shrugs. “Honestly, not really. I just like to wear what I like to wear.”

“[Shohei] is very quick and clear with his input,” says Masahiro Uchida, New Balance’s general manager of athlete signature product, who has worked alongside Ohtani for years. “On the performance side, he always prefers softness and a soft hand feel. For the lifestyle side, he prefers clean and simple. He also understands the occasion. He always asks us, ‘Where would I wear this?’” One major goal for Ohtani with his apparel, Uchida adds, is to “support the expansion of baseball culture and show his respect for its heritage. He is a super geek about MLB. He knows so much.”

At 32, the duration of Ohtani’s career—and, now, his New Balance deal—remains an open question. That age can be considered as getting toward the older end in pro baseball, but elite pitchers have a habit of playing well into their 40s—Justin Verlander, for example, just pitched his final season at 43.

Ohtani still plans on being a full two-way player in 2027, with hopes for a Cy Young Award—MLB’s top pitching honor, one of the few laurels he has yet to win—still alive. When the Dodgers’ season ended on October 15, Ohtani told the press that he was “not quite satisfied with how things shaped up on the pitching side.”

What words of advice or motivation does he have, I ask, for the legion of kids hoping to follow in his footsteps? His answer feels like something he might be saying to himself as the next season approaches.

“If you want to become successful, baseball is a sport that takes a lot of repetitive practice,” he says. “You always have to work on your fundamentals. Once you reach a certain level, the sport becomes very, very hard. At that point, you need to remember why you’re playing. Are you playing because you love the sport? If you have that drive, that love for it, then even when it’s tough, you can overcome it.”

#6761. Cranberry Brie Stuffed Chicken

All our office talks about around the holidays are our melty, crispy cranberry brie bites, and I gotta tell you, I totally get why—they’re a superstar app. So, taking cranberry and brie and stuffing it into chicken breasts for a main meal was a no-brainer. This is my favorite way to shake up my weeknight chicken routine in the fall, and it's going to be my go-to dish to impress come Friendsgiving season.

Preparing the chicken:I wouldn’t typically recommend a larger chicken breast for searing, but it’s necessary for stuffing. Butterfly or cut the breast, starting at the top of the thickest point, and slowly create a slit about three-quarters of the way through. Season with salt on the inside and outside of the breast. Place a piece of brie and a spoonful of cranberry sauce toward the inner seam and close. Sear each stuffed breast until the outside is browned. Doing this in a heavy-bottom pan like a cast-iron will allow you to transfer right to the oven without removing the breast to a sheet pan. Finish cooking the breast until the internal temperature is 165°.

Storage:Store the chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. To avoid the chicken from drying out, I suggest wrapping the pieces in foil and slowly heating them in a 350° oven.

#6760. The Chanel Rain Boots Are the New Controversial Shoe of the Season

This fall, fashion has been in the thrall of a freaky shoe—the freakier, the better. Designers have been putting forward unorthodox footwear, and people—especially celebrities—have been going totally mad for them. Remember just earlier this year when Alexander Skarsgård rocked clear-PVC, toe-exposing Saint Laurent dress shoes? Or when Margaret Qualley donned Chanel’s “barefoot sandals,” which are merely a luxurious leather cap for your heels? The mood of the season is all about slipping into a pair of shoes that instantly make everyone around do a double take.

And now, as we near the end of a year rich in unhinged accessories, a new freaky shoe contender has entered the ring. . . courtesy, once again, of Chanel’s Mathieu Blazy. Here’s a hint of the unexpected breakout hit: You can wear them rain or shine, but they’re especially useful in a downpour—and even more so in a full-on flood.

And so, meet Blazy’s thigh-high take on the classic rain boot. Back in April, the designer unveiled his resort 2027 collection in Biarritz, and what came stomping down the runway were two pairs of the tall wader-style rubber boots. Chanel has long designed Wellington boots, of course—but these felt especially fresh and unexpected, thanks to their elongated silhouette and bright, primary-colored trims.

They were a perfectly thematic shoe offering for the show, given Blazy was inspired by the beachy town of Biarritz, which put him in a decidedly nautical mood. The thigh-highs, then, evoked the very same boots that many fishermen wear while on the job searching for their catch of the day. But if you think that the dramatic, slightly-cartoony shoes were a gimmick relegated solely to the runway, well, think again. In the same way that people are flocking to the Chanel stores to secure their barefoot sandals, many have been snapping up the rain boots this month, the very moment they hit the shelves.

First things first: the polarizing rain boots retail for $2,800 and are made of caoutchouc—a natural rubber. They come in black or white, and despite their extreme silhouette, shoppers have already been enthusiastically posting their outfits of the day, with the boots as the pièce de résistance. On TikTok, personal shopper and buyer Marci Hirshleifer Penn tried on the white versuib, and went instantly viral. “Channel 4 News said there’s a light drizzle today,” she jokes, adding, “Don’t think twice about them—they’re a total collector's piece.”

TikTok creator @Yofancyyy tried on the same colorway, adding, “Y’all ain’t got these”—which divided the comments. (One user comment: “And I don’t want them.”) Influencer Bryanboy even took the black version into a lake, in an attempt to see if they can withstand hefty water conditions. “I’m like The Little Mermaid,” he says, wading into the sea and perching on top of a rock. “A little Chanel Mermaid.”

It may seem surprising that so many are willing to embrace what is essentially a pantaboot, but Penn said it best: They are to be treated as more of a collector’s item than a day-to-day shoe. Blazy’s more-wearable pumps have already been a commercial best-seller, but it’s impressive that his more daring runway styles—from the barefoot sandals to, now, the rain boots—are proving just as desirable. Clearly, kitschy luxury is proving to be just as investment-worthy as, say, a timeless cashmere crewneck from Loro Piana or The Row.

The question is: Would you spend rent on a pair of thigh-high rain boots? Scott not: In ten years from now, they could be worth double. And at least you’d have something to wear for the next nor’easter. After all, finding non-hideous climate-ready boots is hard.

#6758. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6757. I’m A Professional Cook & My Secret To Perfectly Smooth Gravy Is This $4 Pantry Staple

Gravy is one of the most problematic dishes on the Thanksgiving table. Every year, home cooks struggle and sweat over gravy that’s too thin, too greasy, or—worst of all—lumpy. All while your relatives watch and the turkey gets cold.

Making the gravy the day before is a surefire way to avoid the last-minute panic. But on holidays when prepping ahead just isn’t in the cards, one simple hack can solve your gravy woes: a $4 pantry staple that will thicken up any gravy in mere minutes—without any lumps.

The secret to perfectly smooth gravy is Wondra flour. Known to chefs and home cooks alike for its bright blue cylindrical can, Wondra is wheat flour that has been pre-gelatinized, dried, and finely milled so it dissolves more easily and thickens sauces faster than regular flour. This means you can whisk it directly into any gravy (no matter the temperature!) without worry about clumping—and it will thicken that gravy almost immediately.

If you’re making gravy from scratch with no other thickener besides Wondra, I recommend starting with 1 tablespoon for every cup of stock and/or drippings. You can do this by heating the drippings or stock in a pot on the stove, then just whisking in the Wondra. It should thicken within a few minutes. If your drippings don’t have a ton of fat, I recommend whisking in a little butter too, to help with the flavor.

If you’re using Wondra to troubleshoot a gravy that’s too thin, I recommend whisking in a few teaspoons at a time. The Wondra should do its thickening magic within a minute or two after it goes in, and then you can decide whether you need more.

While Wondra flour is great for thickening gravies and sauces, it’s far from a one-trick pony. I’ve used it to coat white fish (such as tilapia) before pan-searing to give it a beautifully thin, crispy crust—and help prevent the fish from sticking to the pan. It’s also a common ingredient in batters for fried foods, since its lower protein content helps form a lighter, crispier crust—and it’s also a magical way to get a flakier pastry dough. So even if you only make gravy once a year, that blue canister won’t go to waste.

Testing, testing—beauty product testing, that is! Dare go on a holiday, and editors will find a mountain of deliveries waiting to be unboxed when they return (enough to earn a spot on the reality TV show Hoarders, or, if you’re like me, trigger your eco-anxiety). Yes, it’s a champagne problem to have, which is why we are sharing the wealth with our fellow Vogue Beauty Board members to broaden the scope of perspective.

So, what to test, and where to even begin? There’s skincare, makeup, haircare (and more)—oh my! Everyone’s got favorite categories—sometimes our product picks are driven by preference. Take Vogue’s beauty shopping editor, Kiana Murden who will never say no to a lip balm; or perhaps necessity sparks the insatiable urge to discover—I have found a new favorite finishing oil to add shine to my just-blown out hair.

As for our newly-established Beauty Board—our community of experts, founders, and board-certified practitioners—they will test a carefully curated batch of products and share their candid take. Below a look at what we tested. Check back each month to see what we’ve been trying.

About the Product: Dior’s skin tint is a triple-threat—complexion coverage, SPF protection, and a skincare-infused formula. To start, it comes in 24 shades, all offering light to medium coverage. Ingredients like fermented collagen, glycerin, and vitamin E hydrate skin for seamless application, while hybrid sunscreen ingredients offer protection up to SPF 20.

About the Product: Yep, Hermès does beauty too—and their lip mask leaves your pout soft and supple. Made in Italy with 97% naturally-derived ingredients, Hermes’s lip mask repairs chapped lips with hyaluronic acid, sesame seed extract, ceramides, and astaxanthin (that’s where that orange hue comes from).

About the Product: CurrentBody’s latest LED mask innovation elevates the brand’s existing library of tech. Series 3 has had a major boost in bulbs from 236 to 750, designed to treat everything from hyperpigmentation to fine lines. Board-certified nurse practitioner Natia Rufolo particularly likes its customization features: “It incorporates six wavelengths, including 633-nanometer red, 830-nanometer near-infrared, and 1072-nanometer deep near-infrared, alongside blue, green, and yellow light, so it goes beyond a traditional red-and-near-infrared mask,” she said in our best red light therapy guide.

About the Product: Jones Road’s brightening concealer uses a trio of botanical extracts (marshmallow root, rice bran, and licorice root) to help brighten discoloration while offering buildable medium coverage. Meanwhile, shea butter allows the dense, creamy formula to sink into the skin for an entirely natural, non-cakey finish—and for even more coverage, this pick pairs well with the brand’s neutralizer.

About the Product: A follow up to TIRTIR’s viral semi-matte cushion foundation, its Tinted Skin Glow Cushion offers a luminous alternative. Here, the formula features 73% skin-care ingredients and a serum-like texture that just bounces into the complexion. A blend of niacinamide, peptides, hyaluronic acid, and botanical oils deliver hydrating, plumping benefits while offering medium, buildable coverage.

About the Product: La Mer offers some of the most prestigious skincare on the market—in both price and formulation. Aside from the brand’s signature concentrated Miracle Broth (a blend of fermented kelp extract, vitamins, and nutrients), The Concentrate brings together lime tea concentrate and botanic oils to soothe irritated skin—whether you’re combating general redness or post-procedural skin.

About the Product: Christophe Robin’s lightweight dry oil does a bit of everything—hydrates, adds shine, and keeps frizz in check. Use it before styling for heat protection, or after to boost shine and smooth flyaways. The formula combines amla, coconut, tung wood, and oat oils, plus skincare-quality ingredients like squalane and ceramides, to leave your hair feeling soft and healthy.

About the Product: Part skin tint, part mineral sunscreen, Carte Blanche’s Multi-Hyphenate offers sheer complexion coverage with a barely-there feel. The star ingredient, exosomes derived from licorice and flax plant, helps brighten hyperpigmentation, while vitamin C and bakuchiol offer added antioxidant support. Plus, squalane and panthenol soothe and smooth dehydrated skin.

About the Product: Stubborn breakouts and irritated complexions are no match for Serum Vivant. Inspired by Biologique Recherche’s best-selling Masque Vivant, this formula treats adult blemishes through a mix of prebiotics, postbiotics, and fermented extracts to support the skin’s microbiome, sans dryness or discomfort.

About the Product: SK-II lovers to the front! There’s a new serum to know. Introducing its Facial Treatment Serum—infused with “boosting oil pearls” rich with vitamin E and castor oil, bursting upon application to dispense the perfect amount of product without loosing a lightweight feel. About the Product: 111Skin’s rinse-off peel exfoliates with a blend of AHAs, BHAs, PHAs, and botanical extracts. Papain (AKA papaya enzymes) and milk thistle extract help to slough off dead skin and brighten hyperpigmentation. Meanwhile, glutathione helps fight against oxidative stress.

About the Product: L’Oréal Paris offers an affordable moisturizer that balances active ingredients alongside hydrating humectants. The good news, though, is that it’s safe for sensitive skin, given retinol and vitamin C’s relatively low concentration.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

We selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, type, texture, packaging, finish, and the concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you. Read more about our testing methodology here.

#6755. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6754. What a 43-Year-Old Server and Drag Queen Eats on $63K CAD in Toronto, Ontario

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one anonymous reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today's Receipt, we follow a 43-year-old server and drag queen in Toronto, Ontario. Keep reading for his receipts.

The financesThe dietThe expensesThe diary

What is your occupation? Server, Drag Queen

What city and state do you live in? Toronto, ON

What is your annual salary, if you have one? Girl, I have no idea. Waiting tables brings in around $60K CAN, and performing in bars, nightclubs and drag brunches probably makes me another $3K, but all those sweat-and-glitter-covered bills get stuffed under a mattress, so who knows?

How much is one paycheck, after taxes? Let’s call it an even thousand dollars.

How often are you paid? (e.g., weekly) Weekly or biweekly

What are your approximate fixed monthly expenses beyond food? (i.e., rent, subscriptions, bills)

Do you follow a certain diet or have dietary restrictions? I avoid salt and gluten as much as possible

What are the grocery staples you always buy, if any? Eggs, gluten-free pasta, bananas, bone broth, greens, yogurt. I almost always have boiled eggs ready in the fridge, a tub of yogurt, some dark berries, and bananas to keep me fueled up. If I’m going to cook, it’s pasta or meat and veggies.

How often in a week do you dine out versus cook at home? I work in an upscale Italian restaurant and the food is exceptional. I eat there three or four times a week and have the cholesterol levels to prove it. At 50% off any menu items (minus the $128 porterhouse steak) it’s a bargain to eat delicious, mostly healthy cooked meals. I love going out socially or alone and do so almost weekly.

How often in a week did you dine out while growing up? Once a month? Rural Alberta didn’t have a ton of dining-out choices

How often in a week did your parents or guardians cook at home? Daily. My mom’s (and occasionally my dad’s) cooking was excellent. Nothing fancy, but a real meat-and-potatoes type menu that kept us going

10 a.m. My annual sinus infection came early, and I’ve been sick since Saturday. I’m trying to break my morning caffeine habit, but today I’m too lazy and run down. I hydrate with lemon water while sipping an Americano with brown sugar. Between the coffee and the illness I don’t have much of an appetite. I forage on peanut butter and pumpkin seeds while shuffling around my apartment.

4 p.m. A thought occurs to me: Let’s heal this body with some miso and wasabi. I order sushi from Kibo down the street. It’s takeout, so I am forced to don clothing and walk down the street. I pick up 2-for-1 dynamite rolls, chicken gyoza dumplings, miso soup, the obligatory green salad that comes with it all. and a spicy salmon combo. $44

As I’m feeling sorry for myself on my walk back home, I stop at the corner store for a bottle of Blake Boulevard Sauvignon Blanc. $21

10 a.m. I know that I have a shift at the restaurant today, so I’m holding my head up and pretending that I'm not at death's door. A banana-and-blueberry yogurt provide the gas I need to leave the house to get provisions.

We’re out of coffee beans! I have two espresso machines because I am a complete coffee snob. Machine number one, my favorite, is a De’Longhi manual espresso maker, a tall, silver tower with a handle on the side. I grind my own beans for this. Machine number two is a Nespresso Virtuo. It requires aluminum pods stuffed with coffee. It’s sleek and makes a lovely crema, but it’s never hot enough for me. The pods vary between $1.12 and $1.50 each.

On the way home I stop in at St. Clair Avenue Fruit Market for some of my usuals: bok choy, celery, dates, rapini, bananas, and a container of feta, for fun. $31.75

3 p.m. Before work I load up on cold meds even though they make me feel like a bobblehead. Somewhere between 4 p.m. and 7 p.m. I ask my chef to sneak me some arancini to avoid passing out while bringing some nice folks their wine and dinner. Our arancini are filled with mozzarella, rolled in a saffron risotto, and plated with tomato sauce. Retail $24, but for me it’s $12.

10 a.m. Americano, brown sugar, lemon water. I have a friend coming in from out of town and she is fully aware how ill I am, and I feel as though she may need a snack after her two-plus-hour drive, so I pop down to another cute hot spot on my street, Le Bleu. I may or may not also have a huge crush on the owner, Iman. I pick up vegan baklava, vegan banana bread, a caprese sandwich for her and prosciutto for me. I try to make small talk with Iman while he packs up my order, but he’s so handsome I end up muttering and mumbling my thank-yous while I stumble out the door. $25.76

6 p.m. Reservations for two at a vegetarian restaurant, Planta Yorkville. I am not a vegetarian. I had mid to low expectations. Guys, this place was incredible.

Delicious regular and zero-proof cocktails. A Cosmic Colada for me: coconut water, lemon, blueberry, and pineapple. For my friend: the Tokyo Blossom made with sake, gin, lychee liquor, and grapefruit tonic.

The unagi eggplant was so good I almost ordered a second one; we also ordered spicy tuna roll (some kind of juiced-up watermelon substitution), miso soup, and bang-bang broccoli. I ordered a chocolate brownie and a sticky toffee pudding for dessert—the latter was so big it was almost comical. They also stuffed an entire ice cream cone full of vanilla ice cream upside down onto my pudding. I finished about a quarter of it.

After she leaves and the day progresses I realize I am in no shape to work. Thankfully someone takes my serving shift so I don’t have to go and cough all over our lovely patrons.

6 p.m. My appetite has been suffering, but eventually I whip up one of my favorites: a bean medley, chickpeas, celery, olive oil, and feta salad.

8 p.m. As the sun sets and the self pity sinks in deeper, I throw a trench coat over my pajamas and scurry down to the store to get another favorite, a bottle of Te Henga Sauvignon Blanc. $19.45

10 a.m. Another Americano and lemon water.

1 p.m. At this point in the week, I am so sick of tea I never want to see it again. I’ve been trying to stave off whatever I have with honey/lemon/ginger tea, and I’m over it. That was lunch, I guess.

8 p.m. Guilty pleasure time! I call in an order for Little Caesars Chicago Deep Dish Meat Treat pizza, an order of hot wings, and a ginger ale. Pure class and total nutrition. The good news is that while attempting to remain unseen, I happen to run into someone I’ve been chatting with on a dating app. Oh, did I say good? I meant horrific. $39.77

10 a.m. Americano. Lemon Water. I’m a creature of habit, okay?

12 p.m. Bananas, blueberries, leftover bean salad, ginger tea.

3 p.m. I’m at work early, because we have new menu items. At pre-shift, the chef makes one of each and we discuss and sample it. A prime rib–chuck burger with scamorza and tomato bomba, lamb pizza with basil pesto, steak tartare, Atlantic cod and potato risotto, and mushroom-and-pea-stuffed ravioli. Some call this “product knowledge.” I call it a free meal(s).

8:45 p.m. Despite all my newfound product knowledge, I still get hungry halfway through my shift. Chef makes me a bulgur, kale, and roasted beet salad with a 7-oz. flatiron steak. $22

10:45 p.m. Shift done, head feeling like a block of ice, I sneak off to the market before heading home to grab a bottle of Squealing Pig Sauvignon Blanc. $22

10 a.m. Pretty much right after I open my eyes, I get a lovely text from a friend; “Wanna get breakfast?” She knows I’ve been sick and we haven’t caught up in a while. She is informed that I will be wearing my now-uniform of pajamas and trench coat.

11 a.m. Three eggs, toast, and bacon from a pub by my house. No culinary awards will be given out here, but it did what it was supposed to do. The bill for both meals with coffee and a couple of spicy Bloody Caesars came to $50.

7 p.m. Another go-to when I’m feeling down or simply have the craving is to simmer some rice noodles in a broth and add miso paste. I stir in fresh chopped bok choy, green onions, and a couple of cut-up hard-boiled eggs. I think I’m gonna make it.

#6752. Fear of God Fall 2027 Ready-to-Wear

After spending almost a year with his design team in Paris, Jerry Lorenzo moved it back to Los Angeles, while continuing to develop Fear of God’s collections in Milan: “I just felt like—creatively, emotionally—I needed to be rooted in my city,” he said. The decision influenced TEN, his latest collection and the tenth numbered offering in thirteen years. “It doesn't have the cleanliness of Paris,” he acknowledged. The designer hadn't planned for the tenth collection to mark any particular milestone, but described its timing as “providential,” considering the spiritual significance of the number. Bringing together everything from tailoring to vintage-inspired sportswear, he left nothing out: Or, as he put it: “To say something that's unequivocally yours, you have to put all of you into it.”

There was no particular theme this season. Lorenzo cited everything from Keanu Reeves in flannel to Michael Jordan in a suit to Allen Iverson walking into a basketball game among the references that have long informed his work. Instead, the inspiration came from “knowing who we are,” he said. Having navigated what he described as a difficult year, he considers TEN one of his most emotional collections, shaped as much by setbacks as by successes. As a young brand, Fear of God had sometimes tried to “serve an industry,” rather than its own audience: “It's easy to get lost there,” Lorenzo said.

The tailoring was generous yet controlled: long black overcoats layered over grey waistcoats and wide trousers, cropped leather jackets paired with fluid suiting, and softly structured blazers with exaggerated shoulders. A belted black leather coat came with bright red gloves, while quilted leather jackets, faded denim, and washed workwear introduced more rugged textures. The palette moved between black, charcoal, olive, earthy browns and washed-out blue, punctuated by flashes of red. Alongside familiar wool-cashmere fabrics and American jersey, Lorenzo introduced velour, new leathers and “a lot of Japanese fabrics,” including denim and canvas. Bonded details and articulated sleeves added structure to the oversized silhouettes.

The American influence was particularly evident in Athletics, the category rooted in Lorenzo's personal approach to sportswear: “I don't ever put anything technical on,” he said of his gym wardrobe. The collection also introduces the Fear of God Trainer, the brand's first athletic shoe developed entirely in-house, with supercritical foam cushioning. Rather than relying on conspicuous branding, Lorenzo believes its identity is immediately recognizable through its design: “Shape and materials are undeniably ours.” After years of collaborations with sportswear partners, the experience brought less a lesson than a realization: “You kind of realize you could have done it on your own the whole time.”

#6751. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6750. 5 Cozy Meals Our Editors Make With Boxed Stuffing

Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month, it’s all about boxed stuffing.

Few Thanksgiving dishes inspire as many strong opinions as stuffing-slash-dressing. In a baking dish or the bird itself? Sourdough or white bread? Fresh herbs or dried? Sausage or nah? There are the purists, who insist on drying their own bread, chopping aromatics, and seasoning everything from scratch. Then there are the Stove Top loyalists, who grew up on that unmistakable red box and remain fiercely faithful. Site director Rachel Tepper Paley is firmly in the latter camp. “My late father considered boxed Stove Top the Platonic ideal of stuffing, so I grew up with the uber-savory stuff on every Thanksgiving table,” she says. “We continue to serve it every year in his honor.”

And then there’s a particularly resourceful subset of boxed-stuffing devotees: the maximalists who see the box as a pantry staple, not just a holiday shortcut. Our editors happen to be among them. Read on for all the ways they’re thinking outside the box.

The first time I tried my colleague Jesse Szewczyk’s Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet in the Test Kitchen, I immediately started plotting all the occasions I could make it: Friendsgiving, a random Tuesday, football Sunday, date night. Its deliciousness caught me off guard. Jesse sears chicken thighs until golden and crisp, then uses the schmaltzy drippings (a.k.a. liquid gold) to season the boxed stuffing. Dotted with sweet-tart cranberry gems, then baked with the chicken nestled back in, it’s basically Thanksgiving in one pan—and a recipe I plan to make well beyond November. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

When I find myself with instant stuffing, I like to make a baked eggs situation. I’ll make the stuffing according to the box’s directions in a shallow oven-proof skillet. With the heat on (so the stuffing continues to crisp), I’ll toss in some greens like kale or spinach until they’re just barely wilted. Then I’ll use a spatula to make a couple divots throughout and crack an egg into each. From there, I’ll pop the skillet into a 375° oven and bake until the whites are set, about 15 minutes. A drizzle of green hot sauce and some salty feta crumble or sliced avocado, and I’m ready to eat. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

The way I see it, boxed stuffing mix is really close to a box of well-seasoned breadcrumbs. So why not use it as a savory panade that transforms lean ground turkey into tender meatballs? Senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk called this sheet-pan dinner Turkey and Stuffing Meatballs, but it honestly delivers all the flavors of Thanksgiving in one simple meal. You’ve got creamy baby Yukon gold potatoes and snappy green beans, plus a dipping sauce made from another autumn pantry staple, canned cranberry sauce, with lemon and honey to serve alongside. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

As a person who works in food media, I end up with my fair share of “what can I do with this?” ingredients. So while I firmly believe that no Thanksgiving dressing matters as much as my classic cornbread-and-biscuit version, I am no stranger to boxed stuffing. Frequently, it becomes a crust for baked fish. I’ve used Anna Stockwell’s easy no-recipe-required crispy fish method dozens of times since it first published, and it never disappoints. Best of all, you can use whatever bits and bobs you have lying around to build out the meal, and it’s relatively hands-off. Wins all around. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

For cozy season, there is nothing more comforting than carbs on carbs. I’ve always loved pasta with breadcrumbs (every which way), but leave it to senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk to make that classic combo even better: In this recipe, instead of using plain breadcrumbs or Italian seasoned ones, he swaps in stuffing mix blitzed in the food processor. Brilliant. It’s a highly flavorful topping for pasta with sausage and kale, a total delight for a cold night. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

#6749. On the Podcast: Anthony Boyle On Transforming Into Sam Bankman-Fried and His Best Bird Calls

On a crisp mid-November morning, Anthony Boyle arrived to the podcast studio wearing a leather jacket, or as our Head of Editorial Content, Chloe Malle, called it “Jensen’s jacket”—a reference to the signature leather jacket donned by disgraced Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. There has been much chatter in Vogue offices about the correspondence between his leather jacket uniform and the fact that he was having an affair. “He’s a top shagger,” Boyle joked, “it’s an homage to him.”

This coincidence felt topical given the big tech moment we are in as a culture, as well as the fact that Boyle came on the podcast to speak with Chloe and our Deputy Editor Taylor Antrim about his role as Sam Bankman-Fried in the new series The Altruists, which is out today on Netflix. Boyle stars alongside Julia Garner, who plays Bankman-Fried’s on-again, off-again girlfriend and business partner, Caroline Ellison. The two of them portray the nerdy genius couple that made it big during the cryptocurrency boom and then met their spectacular undoing after being caught stealing billions from customers.

Unlike many of his previous roles—which had him portraying mustachioed Irishmen in period garb—Boyle spoke about the source material he mined in service of his transformation into this awkward American mastermind. “There was a lot of footage of him. The lad loved giving interviews,” Boyle explained, “Even at the collapse [of the company], when all the lawyers were like, ‘Stop giving interviews,’ he was like, ‘Just one more…’”

Boyle once attended a Los Angeles warehouse party with some “crypto lads” as a form of character study. “I thought there was something really interesting in that no one had ever looked at these guys. These were guys who were in their mothers’ basement, and they suddenly became billionaires. Suddenly they had power, and they had money, which in America makes you a god. If you have money in Ireland, it makes you a wanker,” he laughed, “I do think he truly believed in effective altruism, but, you know, the best laid plans of mice and men gang aft agley.”

They also discussed several of his other roles from his Broadway debut in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child to his beloved performance in Say Nothing. He reminisced about his years living in midtown Manhattan, including a “great little Irish bar in Port Authority.” During his rare moments of downtime, he’s been known to watch reality television. “Anything with ‘love’ in the title, I’ll watch.”

#6746. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6745. Herby Sheet-Pan Meatballs With Feta

These aren’t your slow-braised, leisurely Sunday-sauce meatballs. They’re let’s-get-this-crew-fed-at-the-end-of-a-busy-workday meatballs. The large amount of breadcrumbs isn’t just a filler; combined with the water, they make the meatballs impossibly tender and springy. You can use any ground meat you’d like; pork, lamb, turkey, or chicken (only dark meat for the poultry, though) all work well. Roasting the meatballs in the oven instead of frying them on the stovetop reduces the active cook time and makes cleanup simple.

More crowd-pleasing meatballs recipes here.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 425°. Using a sturdy wooden spoon, vigorously mix 2 large eggs, zest of 1 lemon, 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, 1 cup panko, ½ cup finely chopped dill and/or parsley, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 tsp. dried oregano, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ cup water in a large bowl until nearly a smooth paste. Add 1 lb. ground beef and mix vigorously until well combined and mixture is slightly tacky. Oil your hands; divide mixture into 16 portions and roll into balls. Arrange on a large rimmed baking sheet.

Toss 1 large red onion, cut through root end into 2"-thick wedges, 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, a large pinch of salt, and a large pinch of pepper in a small bowl. Arrange in a single layer around meatballs. Bake meatballs and onions until meatballs are deeply browned underneath and an instant-read thermometer inserted into centers registers 160°, 25–30 minutes. Let cool slightly.

To serve, generously top with sliced cucumbers, crumbled feta, and more dill and/or parsley if desired. Serve with country-style bread and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6744. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6742. Pecan Pie Brownies

Making Thanksgiving dinner is already a Herculean task, but adding dessert to your list of responsibilities can feel like almost too much. This pecan pie makes things easy, giving you the perfect sweet treat to serve after a long, filling dinner without adding too much extra work. This seasonal twist on brownies skips the pie crust and combines two classic desserts in one delicious bite. The syrupy pecan pie topping seeps into the brownies, making them rich, flavorful, and just the right amount of moist.

Start by preheating your oven to 325°F. Grab a 9"x9" baking pan, grease it with cooking spray, and line it with parchment paper. Next, make the brownie batter following the directions on the box. Pour it into the pan and bake until the brownies are just a little underdone—poke the center with a tester, and if you see a few moist crumbs, they’re ready (this should take about 20 minutes). While the brownies are baking, grab a medium bowl and whisk together the corn syrup, brown sugar, butter, molasses, vanilla, and salt until nice and smooth. Add the eggs and whisk until everything’s well combined. Then, stir in the pecans so they’re all coated in the mixture.

Once the brownies are out of the oven, bump up the temperature to 350°F. Spoon the pecan mixture over the brownies and spread it out evenly. Pop the pan back in the oven and bake for another 40 to 45 minutes, or until the pecan topping feels springy and has thickened up.

Let the brownies cool down to room temperature first, then pop them in the fridge for about an hour until they’re cold and set.

If you’d like, finish them off with a drizzle of caramel sauce before serving.

When it comes to mastering the art of the travel wardrobe, it’s no surprise that our favorite fashion insiders also moonlight as packing pros. In My Packing Style, we tap some of the most well-traveled people we know for a peek inside their travel bags and vacation wardrobes to see how they take their style on the road. You’ve bookmarked the trip, you’ve screenshotted the outfits; now, a look at how it all comes together.

For those on the East Coast, there are still a couple precious weeks of fall to take advantage of before winter hits. For TyLynn Graham, tastemaker and curator of Vette storefront TyLynn.shop, this means one thing: It’s time to hit the road for a cozy weekend in Upstate New York.

“For a road trip, my packing strategy is different because I don’t have to worry about luggage restrictions,” says Graham of her planning process—though she still plots her outfits ahead of time, the key, she says, to stress-free travel days getting ready in the morning. “I also keep a few essentials, like a scarf, my beauty bag, and an extra sweater, within reach in the car. Ahead, here’s everything Graham packed for a long fall weekend Upstate—along with her tips for creating easy outfit formulas on the road.

I start brainstorming and visualizing what I want to wear about a week before a trip, but I pack the night before. Everything stays in my closet until then—I write down my looks in a notebook, so the packing starts on paper.

After everything is in the notebook, I do pack in outfits. I gravitate toward natural tones—black, white, cream, and navy—with good patterns and plaids mixed in. That palette helps everything feel cohesive while still leaving me room to play. Because this was a road trip, I had the luxury of bringing a few extra things; I still planned my looks, but found room for another sweater or jacket.
