#6718. Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

"It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?"

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently."

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”

"Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

#6717. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6716. Is Merch Stealing Luxury’s Aspirational Consumer?

Typically, middle-income young shoppers have focused their fashion spending on accessible luxury goods or one-off splurges, like a Coach Tabby bag ($375) or a Longchamp Le Pliage ($165).

However, among these groups, a growing faction is trading down, looking instead to the fast-developing category of merch to broadcast their affiliation to culture, whether it’s the newly launched Rhode windbreaker ($257) or last week’s frenzied release of a hot-pink GTA logo tee ($66). While merch is nothing new in the fashion market — Balenciaga relied heavily on it during Demna’s tenure between 2015 and 2025 — the playing field is changing, with a stronger focus on the temporal buzz of a new digital or game-based craze, the cult movie everyone’s watching, the fiendishly anticipated alt-rap tour, or a new milestone in a girl-boss beauty community’s trajectory — like Rhode founder Hailey Bieber’s 30th birthday.

“Brands invest inordinate amounts of resources into product research and development to try and catch the ever-elusive hype cycle. But with [consumers] suddenly coveting more transient ‘merchandise’ over main line product ranges, is that investment misplaced?” asks Simon Richardson, group strategy director at creative agency Amplify. “What [brands] should be doing is creating a moment in time, not just a product line. Fans need more — all the time — to signal what they care about in a way that feels distinct, real and truly of a moment.”

Recently, Jordan Firstman, director of buzzy gay drama Club Kid, called on New York designer Emily Dawn Long — renowned among Dimes Square it-kids for her in-the-know screenprinted vintage tees — to design the merch for the film. The designer, known for her Spoiled Boys slogan tee, emblazoned the ragged tops with one of the film’s lines, “It’s like that every time”. In the film itself, Firstman also wore his own Emily Dawn Long tee, printed with the words, “Take off your clothes”. On Wednesday, A24 took over a downtown 1<3 NY souvenir shop to sell the capsule, before releasing a limited online drop (most styles are sold out).

A24 worked with designer Emily Dawn Long for new film Club Kid’s merch.

Tech bros are also tapping in. This year, Trump-contracted data surveillance firm Palantir released a chore jacket ($239) not dissimilar to those purveyed by cult restaurants, such as Sessions Arts Club and St. John. Reportedly, the company’s broader apparel line is performing, especially in South Korea, where the windbreaker ($170) sold out. Much-talked-about corporation Nvidia — whose CEO Jensen Huang stepped down this week following his extramarital affair with a potential Chinese spy — also released a sweater emblazoned with a leather-jacketed cartoon of Huang ($178). The design is picking up strong resale value again following the scandal: one seller listed the design on Ebay for $2,500. And OpenAI offers a racing-style shirt ($75) not dissimilar to styles from Corteiz, Palace and Supreme — as well as bumper stickers ($10) and caps ($40), all sold on its website.

As luxury struggles to justify its price hikes — since the average price of personal luxury goods increased by 52% between 2019 and 2024, per HSBC — the merch market has swooped in to capitalize on the aspirational shopper. In the US, consumer sentiment is low, and yet spending is up. Indeed, across the US, Europe and China, shoppers are more cautious and discerning with discretionary purchases, guided by a brand’s value propositions. If a band tee, a Roblox hoodie, or a pair of GTA x Travis Scott Nike Air Force 1 sneakers can communicate cultural belonging, community adjacency, and lifestyle for a fraction of the cost of a luxury handbag, then merch wins.

Indeed, in late 2025, 72% of Gen Z luxury shoppers told Vogue Business they would prefer owning a Walmart “Wirkin” over a genuine Hermès Birkin, and when interviewed, several respondents said they deem spending lots of money on luxury distasteful and that luxury goods are not worth the cost. At the same time, beauty continues to boom with aspirational shoppers, but — unlike clothing and accessories — has only a handful of ways to turn its goods into walking advertisements. The Rhode phone case, seen in influencer selfies, marked the first step towards a solution, then came the wearable merch. Similarly, tech giants largely deal in intangible goods. But physical merch is a way for fans to display their favorite chip-maker or AI platform.

Hailey Bieber wears her new Rhode windbreaker, which retails at $257.

For beauty, and even tech, merch gives brand fans a way to express their appreciation of the products and the communities around them. Companies recognize young people’s appetite to feel part of something.

Millennial readers will remember when “merch” referred primarily to band T-shirts. That playbook began in musical subcultures and has now transferred to a broader market. “Gen Alpha grew up inside worlds. For them, a ‘skin’ [Fortnite’s in-game outfits] is merch, a creator’s snack bar is merch, and a hoodie is the physical version of a world they already spend hours in,” says Jolyon Varley, co-founder of marketing agency OK Cool.

“Logos used to confer status and were a more reliable indicator of what you could afford or how you were living,” he adds. “Merch tells people what you’re into, and that’s become far more valuable. It’s a matter of signaling taste rather than wealth.”

Varley points to the frenzy seen at GTA’s Selfridges launch, explaining that consumers now associate with much more than simply products, but instead entire worlds. “GTA isn’t just a game any more,” he says. “Millions of people live in it. The launch week proved it.”

Whether that’s an event exclusive, an IP artefact made real for the ‘heads’, or even a staff uniform, exclusivity and experience are major drivers of hype, says Amplify’s Richardson. “Something that says, ‘I was there’, not just ‘this is what I’m into’.”

Richardson also notes that fandom thrives on shared codes and signals. So his advice for brands wanting a piece of the pie? “Bringing together your own lore, something that anchors your merch in time, and the right collaborators to bring it to life in a fan-first and agile way, can turn a small run of products into a mass-reach driver.” The Rockstar Games’s GTA takeover of Miami — a reported $3.9 million deal with Miami-Dade County — sets the bar, lighting up Miami Heat’s stadium, dressing players in black-and-pink jerseys, and activating across the city.

Merch’s appeal lies in the power of the brand and what that communicates. It’s a quick win to cross categories, too. “If you build a brand that is cool, interesting, culturally relevant, aspirational, it [almost] doesn’t matter what you’re selling, because what you’re selling is the aura — this ineffable, ‘it’, cool factor,” says Ursula founder and brand strategist Emma Hope Allwood. “Just practically, when you have these big cultural moments or launches like GTA, it makes sense to try to break it down into different categories — different ways for people to be part of it, rather than it just being a game.”

Luxury brands that want to re-enter the merch market and cultural players looking to seize the growing momentum need to broach the sector carefully. “Not all merch is cool,” says Sara McAlpine, co-founder of brand and marketing studio Bikini, highlighting the recent tech brand plays. “There’s no reason to be producing a chore coat unless you’re trying to say you’re aligned with a Carhartt WIP and Japanese-denim wearing aesthetic-conscious crowd.”

So what works? Influencer and DJ Leo Mandella visited the GTA Selfridges pop-up. He typically doesn’t consider merch cool — “[it] can look a bit gimmicky” — but the capsule delivered, he believes. “It’s very easy for gaming companies to mess up on the rest of the promo run, but Rockstar were absolutely incredible at creating a capsule of merch that was just as good as the game,” says Mandella, who spent £250 (roughly $329) at the pop-up. “I think merch is especially exciting when done well because you feel part of a moment. It’s not just a piece of clothing. Buying a Vice City tee or a Burger Shot uniform [the official in-game restaurant chain] makes you feel like you’re in this fictional world.”

Nonetheless, for brands that still want to communicate esotericism, merch remains an astute method. Varley pinpoints the power of releasing one-off, friends-and-family T-shirts during events. He cites the Awake x Jordan T-shirts — art directed by London graffiti artist Fatzoo — given out during Notting Carnival at the Deviation stage. “That immediately orients you in a specific nucleus of that scene,” he says. “If you weren’t there — or don’t know the individuals involved — you didn’t get one.”

#6715. Listen to BA Bake Club's Podcast on Salt Bread

Imagine a Parker House roll having a tryst with Asian-style milk bread and a classic French croissant—that’s the essence of salt bread, a.k.a. shio pan in Japan and sogeum-ppang in Korea.

“These little buns…they look so cute, but they are so rich,” guest contributor, and our deputy food editor, Hana Asbrink explains to BA Bake Club hosts Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic. “You can really just snack on them solo and be so satisfied.”

This month’s episode is also more bittersweet than usual, as Shilpa reveals that she is leaving Bon Appétit to take on new projects. “I’m so proud of Bake Club,” Shilpa says. “Thank you to all of our readers and listeners. You really have made this the most wholesome corner of the internet and my career.”

We can’t let her go without a proper send off. Follow Shilpa on Instagram to see what comes next in her baking adventures. And fret not, BA Bake Club will continue full steam ahead with Jesse at the helm!

We’d love to hear from you! Send your questions to BA Bake Club on Substack or send a voice memo or email to [email protected].

SU: We're both senior test kitchen editors at Bon Appétit.

SU: Every month we publish a recipe on bonappetit.com that introduces a baking concept that we think you should know.

#6713. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6712. Katie Holmes’s Holiday Party Trick? Matching Her Lipstick to Her Bag

A flash of red is a holiday party classic, and Katie Holmes is making a persuasive case for doubling down on the festive color. The actor stepped out in New York for a holiday celebration hosted by Meiomi Pinot Noir, with her boyfriend Jason Bard Yarmosky by her side, serving up a masterclass in laidback party dressing.

While fellow guests embraced the season’s faux fur, feathers, and sequins, Holmes stuck to her trusty winter uniform: a sweeping black coat from Lafayette 148 layered over a simple white top and dark Banana Republic corduroys, with black shoes by The Row. The pièce de résistance was a cherry-red Gucci shoulder bag, perfectly coordinated with her punchy red lipstick.

It’s an easy styling trick, but an effective one. The two flashes of crimson brought a festive sensibility to an otherwise pared-back ensemble, while the lipstick also felt particularly appropriate for an evening celebrating Pinot Noir. Holmes looked very much in the holiday spirit, without a sequin in sight.

Of course, Katie Holmes is something of an It-bag enthusiast: a classic quilted Chanel 19 Flap Bag, the sleek Private Eye bag by Métier, the trapezoid Akris Ai shoulder bag, an iconic Celine Triomphe, a suite of Ferragamo. Her extensive rotation runs from roomy everyday totes to polished, structured shoulder bags, often serving as the focal point of her otherwise uncomplicated outfits. She has a knack for making even the most coveted accessories look effortless, pairing them with straight-leg denim jeans and louche tailoring.

And then there’s her enduring affection for a red lip. Holmes has long understood its transformative powers, particularly when paired with her favored minimal makeup and swept-back hair. Here, with her dark hair neatly pulled back, the bold lipstick was allowed to do the talking.

Matchy-matchy glam has been all over the celebrity circuit: everyone from Taylor Swift to Kylie Jenner is choosing coordinating mani-pedis in deep shades of seasonal onyx and Bordeaux, while Jennifer Lopez embraced all-over burgundy.

Forget matching your bag to your shoes. This holiday season, Katie Holmes proves matching it to your makeup can be a true festive delight. And, as demonstrated here, you don’t have to sacrifice comfort—or your favorite corduroys—to look party-ready.

#6710. The Best Cast-Iron Skillets for a Lifetime of Cooking (2026)

For some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet. There is a die-hard fan base loyal to the affordable US-made Lodge cast-iron pan that will not hear of any other suggestions.

There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

To these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”

If you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t; either way, I’m happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

Cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be said for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

Yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think, and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

And cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a burnished crispy exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast iron alongside its stainless-steel and carbon steel pans and enameled Dutch oven.

New in this update: A review of Made In's new cast-iron pan as well as more long-term testing information for our winner.

Size(s): 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes

What I loved: Because they’re much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the new era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small company based in Southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

The Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 lb. for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 lb. or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly big difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

It has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron, though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes pre-seasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties, though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

Other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

An earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

What I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I’ll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

In the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn’t that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I’ve found that this doesn’t impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

Below you’ll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn’t have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some gray patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won’t hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don’t let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you’re really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff off the excess, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

Some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it’s a record of use and proof that it’s growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you’re just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

If you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

Size(s): 4.8" (1.1 lb.), 6.5" (2 lb.), 8" (3.1 lb.), 10" (5.5 lb.), 12" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes

What I loved: Again, I apologize for snubbing Lodge, as even in our office we have a number of staunch brand loyalists. But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are pre-seasoned with flaxseed oil and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough pre-seasoning is more important on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. But we know that some people want as much of a head start as they can get, and this pan offers you the best one.

The other way the Victoria bested the Lodge is in its form factor. The pour spouts on the Victoria are nice and wide, making it easy to pour off oil or other pan juices, and testers found the handle shape slightly more comfortable than the Lodge.

I’ll be honest, though, these differences are pretty small, and if you feel drawn to the Lodge name, I recommend it as well.

What I’d leave: Given it’s bargain pricing, there isn’t much to dislike here. I will note this pan is significantly heavier than the Lancaster pan—a full pound and a half for the same diameter skillet. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it’s a trade-off you’ll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

1. We had several members of staff handle the pans to get a broad sense of how easy the pans were to maneuver. Then we got to cooking.

2. Using a little bit of oil, we fried eggs sunny-side up and scrambled to see how much (if anything) stuck to the pan.

3. We seared skin-on chicken thighs to get a sense of how evenly heat was distributed around the cooking surface. We also measured how long it took for the pan to reach 375° at medium heat.

4. We washed the pans in hot water, noting any places where seasoning might have worn away.

5. We re-seasoned the pans ourselves in an oven for an hour at 500°.

6. We cooked another round of eggs to observe any changes.

I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

Sizing is a bit different from company to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we’re talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

Heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon steel frying pans get hot quickly, but they don’t always have the heat-retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear safely with them.

The Stargazer is a lovely pan. Like the Lancaster, its a vintage-style skillet, so it has a smooth texture that’s easy to clean. The surface develops seasoning well, and the curved lip allows for easy pouring at any angle. Ultimately, it is one of the heavier high-end skillets available on the market, which is why we don’t have it as a winner. However, if weight isn’t a huge concern for you, it is still an excellent pan.

If you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a new name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. This pan has a nice velvety surface that holds on to seasoning very well, while still maintaining a smooth, glossier finish that makes vintage-style pans so desirable. Small gripes: The handle design wasn’t a favorite among testers, and the side walls are a slightly shorter than most other cast-iron pans. It’s also a touch heavier and a couple touches more expensive than our winner. Still, this is an excellent cast-iron pan and makes a great family heirloom.

Lodge Cast-Iron Skillet with Red Mini Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 8"

People who track recommendations like these tend to be shocked that we don’t place the Lodge as our winner or budget pick. It is a fantastic pan, make no mistake. It has a great factory seasoning that’s resilient from the jump, and the 10" costs around twenty bucks—so what gives? When it came down to it, the Victoria pan had a slicker factory seasoning out of the box and a more comfortable handle design.

Another high-end polished cast-iron pan on the list. Smithey pans are gorgeous, so much so that it almost feels wrong cooking with them. However, you should cook with it straight away, as the factory seasoning is a little light on these, and we observed a little bit wearing away after the first couple rounds of cooking prior to us adding an additional layer of seasoning. Senior editor Noah Kaufman has been cooking with the Smithey multiple times a week for a couple years and says that within a few months of regular use and two bouts of seasoning in the oven he no longer worried about stuck eggs or steaks.

Gorgeous as they are, Smithey pans are heavy, though, at 5.8 lb. for the 10" skillet.

This skillet is the second lightest (4.3 lb. at 10") and has a velvety surface that holds on to seasoning a little better than the smooth polished pans. Like the Stargazer, it also has a curved lip instead of a pour spout, but I found that this pan does have a bit of a dribbling problem, which I wasn't crazy about. Still, one member of our team who has now lived with this pan for years loves it and uses it every day.

Lodge Cast-Iron Blacklock Skillet, Triple Seasoned - 10.25"

Lodge released this pan in response to the wave of new and fancy polished pans, and as beautiful (quite beautiful), well-seasoned (three glossy layers), and lightweight as it is (almost even with the Lancaster), our testers found the handle uncomfortable to hold.

Ooni is a pizza oven company, and this pan is really designed for cooking in an oven rather than on the stovetop. It has a detachable handle, which is actually a genius bit of design that makes it easy and comfortable to grab out of a blazing hot pizza oven. But the sides are too shallow for doing more normal cast-iron things like frying chicken or sautéing greens. It is, however, great for cornbread and pizookies.

This is Made In’s official entry into the cast-iron new wave. The pan has a smooth machined surface, nice design touches, like curved sidewalls and a spacious helper handle. The primary handle is nice to hold; however, a longer handle can make a pan feel heavier and add strain on the wrists. This pan is not the lightest, either. I found it difficult to transport the full pan from the stovetop to the oven using only one hand, so consider this a pan for people with meaty forearms. Made In also uses flaxseed oil for the factory seasoning, which is a controversial choice in the cast-iron world. The reason for that controversy is that, while the finish flaxseed oil produces is glossy and attractive, it tends to be brittle. Especially with newer pans, a flaxseed seasoning has a tendency to wear away with regular cooking. After testing, I did notice this pan had some gray (unseasoned) patches after a round of searing meat. Again, not a big deal—just keep cooking with it— but something to keep in mind. All of that being said, I do still think this is a high-quality pan. During the cooking tests, I had absolutely no issues with sticking whatsoever.

This pan is pretty similar to a standard Lodge or Victoria, but with a seasoning that’s not as nonstick out of the box. We did find, however, that it added new layers of seasoning quite well.

The Valor is apparently a favorite in restaurants, but there’s nothing special to it that makes it stand out. If anything, the pour spouts are so small they might as well not be there at all.

We’re all for innovation, which is what Finex sought to do with its octagonal pan and its bulbous handle, but we didn’t really observe any value from the modifications. While the octagonal shape is easier for flipping you could just use a bigger cast-iron pan for anything you want to flip. And its “speed cool” handle was awkward to hold.

Anytime KitchenAid ventures beyond the small appliance space you never quite know what you’re gonna get. In this case, it’s a cast-iron pan that is totally average in every way, except for its minimalist modern design. We think this pan is too expensive for what you’re getting.

“Ooh, a lid!” Was the universal reaction to this cast-iron pan. If you like the idea of having a lid for your pan, then this is your pan. The problem with cast-iron lids, though, is that they don’t benefit from the progressive seasoning development the rest of the pan gets as you cook with it. Lids are only really dealing with evaporative moisture, which makes them even more likely to rust. Smithey, up above, sells glass lids that fit their pans, which, while not as oven-safe, won’t have that rust problem.

This is Victoria’s answer to the high-end polished cast-iron pan. The seasoning is great, but the pan is heavier than the Lancaster, and we didn’t love all the extra design embellishments. The brass insert on the handle had no practical value (it heated up quicker than the surrounding cast iron). Also, all the extra ridges and divots just meant more places for gunk to get stuck in.

Amazon customers really like this pan. It comes with a silicone handle cover and a glass lid, which is nice (glass is a better material for a lid than cast iron). It also has tall 3" sides that make this pan great for frying. Beyond that, though, the pan is heavy and seemed to be barely pre-seasoned.

This is a super polished cast-iron pan with a glossy cooking surface that was nice to work with. However, we noticed quite a few cosmetic issues, like small nicks and rough edges that made it seem like there were some corners cut in the manufacturing process.

Another pan that is just fine. The factory seasoning is minimal, so you’ll have to build that up yourself. There are several better options that are just as affordable from Victoria, Lodge, and others.

This is an affordable pan that looks a lot like a Lodge, but with a lesser factory seasoning.

The seasoning that came on this pan out of the box was pretty bad, and with so many other cheap alternatives that offer much better quality, we don’t see the point in purchasing this pan. It’s also only available in a 15" diameter at the time of writing, which is bigger (and heavier) than most people need.

When you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as pre-seasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

No, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.)

For really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.)

If, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

Wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit’s resident cookware tester and researcher for over six years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a big apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

#6709. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6708. The Vogue Business Beauty Trend Tracker

The Vogue Business Beauty Tracker, produced in collaboration with Spate, tracks the top five brands, trends and ingredients that are driving the most significant positive change in year-on-year growth that have also demonstrated consistent upward growth historically. Each week, we’ll spotlight a different beauty category and the top five beauty hashtags on TikTok.

It’s all about the multi-purpose fragrance this week as search data highlights growing interest in fragrances that combine practical formats, occasion-led scents, and distinctive notes. Searches for Chanel’s Coco Mademoiselle Fragrance Primer reflect demand for prep products that extend a scent’s wear, projection, and hold on the skin. Travel fragrance shows continued interest in travel-size versions of full-size scents. Meanwhile, wedding fragrance reflects demand for a dedicated signature scent for the big day, and white floral perfume highlights interest in scents built around blossoms such as jasmine, gardenia, and tuberose, while pineapple fragrance signals demand for bright, tropical fruit notes.

For fragrance brands, there is growing interest in concept-driven scents, heritage expertise, and affordable fragrance lines. Lore fragrances inspire specific memories, moods, and places, while Toskovat, an independent niche perfume house from Romania, stands out for composing each scent as a “bottled memory”, or extrait de mémoire. Shiseido reflects interest in the Japanese house’s heritage fragrances, with searches focused on Zen. Ranger Station, based in Nashville, draws on music culture and American landscapes for its unisex, artisan-style scents. Finally, Old Navy points to demand for affordable fragrance through Old Navy Beauty Co., its line of hair and body mists, lotions, and body washes, which expanded in August 2026.

It’s all about hair and nail maintenance on TikTok this week.

#KTipHairExtension reflects interest in semi-permanent extensions, with stylists showing how individual strands are bonded to natural hair using keratin tips. #CurlyHairGel and #CurlyHairVolume highlight interest in curly hair styling, from gels that keep curls defined, hydrated, and frizz-free to techniques that build lift and fullness at the root. #HolidayEyeMakeup points to interest in festive, party-ready eye looks, with tutorials circulating ahead of the winter holidays. Meanwhile, #CuticleRemover centers on at-home nail care, with videos demonstrating how to use Sally Hansen’s Instant Cuticle Remover.

At-home application and retro, graphic designs are among this month’s biggest nail trends. Searches for solid gel polish are on the rise, reflecting demand for a thicker, pot-based gel formula designed for more controlled application, while press-on sets remain popular for their reusability. White chrome powder, which creates a pearly, mirror-like finish when buffed over gel polish, is trending in time for the winter months, as well as geometric nail designs for their clean lines and shapes. Meanwhile, vintage nail polishes, including Urban Decay’s discontinued metallic foil shades, reinforce consumer interest in discontinued products that allow for a nostalgic aesthetic.

For nail brands, DIY manicure solutions, art-driven designs, and everyday nail tools are proving a success. The rise of Cyprus-based brand Doonails reflects demand for do-it-yourself manicure and pedicure products designed to deliver salon-quality results. Never Have I Ever reflects demand for reusable press-on nails featuring licensed artwork from independent artists and cultural icons, while Double Rhythm underscores interest in accessible soak-off gel polishes and nail art supplies. Heyhae offers sun-cured gel nail strips that harden naturally in sunlight without requiring a traditional UV or LED lamp, and Diamond Cosmetics signals continued interest in accessible nail products that offer variety and affordability.

Hair how-to content is ever-growing on TikTok, with creators twisting small sections of coily hair into a #coiltwist or #CurlsWithStraightener tutorials doing the rounds. Meanwhile, the rise in videos showing off #DarkBalayage points to demand for soft, dimensional color finishes on brunette and black hair, which offers a subtle look that minimizes root visibility. There’s also rising demand for lip stains that provide #AllDayLipColor, while #TestingMakeup content shows creators trying out new viral products in their full-face routines, sharing verdicts as they go.

The makeup products consumers are searching for the most are those combining precise application, long wear, and shimmering finishes. Tools such as winged eyeliner stamps take the stress and guesswork out of creating a sharp, even cat-eye look, while creamy lip liners offer buildable definition through soft, blendable formulas. Gripping primers and longwear lipsticks also reflect demand for staying power, from tacky primers that give makeup a sticky base to lip formulas designed to resist fading and transfer. Meanwhile, the rise of rose gold eyeshadow highlights interest in pink-toned metallic shades that add dimension to eye looks.

When it comes to makeup brands, lasting interest in Burberry Beauty signals the strength of luxury cosmetics from established fashion houses, especially foundations. Nude by Nature highlights demand for makeup powered by natural Australian botanicals. Beauty Creations, a Latina-founded brand, stands out for high-pigment formulas, frequent limited-edition collections, and pop culture partnerships. Sculpted by Aimee, founded by makeup artist Aimee Connolly, reflects interest in multitasking, skin-first products that simplify daily routines. Finally, KeyYou points to demand for lash extension kits and cluster lashes designed for self-application.

There’s a demand for the nostalgic on TikTok, with the #ThrowBackBeauty hashtag showing creators recreating and reviewing makeup, hair, and fashion looks from past decades. Over on #PerfumeTok, the fragrance community is reviewing, ranking, and recommending scents, while #BlackFridayBeautyDeals points to anticipation ahead of TikTok Shop’s official Black Friday campaign. Meanwhile, #FalseLashesTutorial reflects demand for step-by-step guidance on applying false lashes, and #ServerHairInspo highlights low-maintenance hairstyles built to last throughout the work shift — fueled by the viral “server hair theory” that certain styles can earn servers higher tips.

Skincare products that combine regenerative ingredients, targeted application, and everyday hydration are on the rise in search. Fresh PDRN formats — creams, face masks, and eye patches — reinforce interest in the ingredient, which is associated with cellular repair and a stronger skin barrier, as well as its use in targeted treatments like the Abib PDRN Retinal Eye Patch. Increased searches for hyaluronic acid face lotion reflects demand for deep hydration in everyday skincare, while liquid pimple patches highlight interest in subtle formulas that directly target blemishes and dry into an invisible film.

Skincare consumers are particularly intrigued in brands combining clinical-grade formulas, advanced delivery technologies, and everyday sun protection. Magic Molecule reflects continued demand for hypochlorous acid, offering a multi-purpose, FDA-cleared spray for everyday skincare. KRX Aesthetics and Meditherapy, both South Korean brands, are known for their professional skin treatments adapted for at-home use. Radical Skincare stands out for its performance-driven anti-aging formulas, powered by its proprietary Trylacel delivery technology. Finally, Invisible Zinc reflects demand for mineral-based sunscreens that use zinc oxide as the primary ingredient instead of chemical UV filters.

Over on TikTok, #DolphinSkin reflects interest in ultra-glossy, smooth, and luminous skin, specifically on the body. #GreenChromeNails and #ColorLashes highlight bold approaches to color, from mirror-like metallic manicures in shades of green to multi-colored lash looks. Content featuring #TTSKbeauty, or TikTok Shop K-beauty, shows the platform’s growing role in K-beauty product discovery. Meanwhile, the rise of #JasmineFragrance is driven by Chun Breeze Xian Jasmine, a Chinese fragrance that creators compare to the jasmine tea scent of tea house chains Molly Tea and Heytea.

In haircare, products that combine scalp support, deep nourishment, and targeted cleansing are trending in search. Peptide hair serums cater to those seeking lightweight formulas that support fuller-looking hair, with searches associated primarily with The Ordinary’s Multi-Peptide Serum for Hair Density, while hair thinning serums points to a broader focus on density and scalpcare. Rice water hair spray highlights interest in a convenient leave-in format for an ingredient valued for adding strength and shine. Cholesterol hair treatment reflects demand for rich, deep-conditioning masks that restore moisture and softness, and chlorine removal shampoo signals demand for clarifying formulas that remove chlorine build-up post-swim.

When it comes to brands, the rise of K-beauty player Lilyeve reflects demand for daily scalpcare, with searches led by its Scalp Turn Cica PDRN Brush Ampoule, a cooling leave-in treatment applied through a built-in brush head. Demand for Honeyque products highlights interest in salon-grade Japanese haircare designed to repair dry, damaged and frizzy hair, while Chāmpo stands out for blending ayurvedic principles with modern trichology, particularly through its hair serum. Bare Anatomy underscores continued demand for science-backed, dermatologically tested haircare, from anti-dandruff shampoo to a roll-on scalp serum. Finally, Brickell Men’s Products reflects interest in natural grooming formulated specifically for men.

Beyond traditional beauty content, #MakeupGame on TikTok reflects the growing overlap between beauty and gaming, with posts centered around Makeup Mania, a Roblox game where players compete through makeup and fashion looks. #HowToSilkPress and #4CWashDay highlight continued demand for textured hair education, from step-by-step silk press tutorials to wash day routines tailored to tightly coiled 4C hair. The #GlitterAcrylic hashtag points to interest in sparkling, statement acrylic nail sets, while #EczemaPatch shows the hydrocolloid format popularized by pimple patches expanding to eczema-prone skin.

In the wellness world, there’s growing interest in specialized nutrition and brands that prioritize convenience and targeted health benefits. Pure Genius Protein reflects demand for portable, high-protein formats, with ready-to-drink shots providing 23 grams of protein per serving. Sisel highlights a broad approach to wellness through dietary supplements and functional beverages, while Toplux Nutrition emphasizes science-backed supplements at affordable prices. Wip stands out for its nicotine-free caffeine pouches, offering a convenient format for an energy boost. Finally, Triquetra Health reflects interest in gut and metabolic wellness, with searches focused on its GLP-Pro probiotic and postbiotic supplement. Collectively, these brands span everyday protein intake, energy support, and targeted nutritional supplementation.

In the midst of October, #HalloweenHairClips are trending on TikTok, reflecting interest in festive, spooky hair accessories — particularly horror-themed claw clips and seasonal designs. Meanwhile, the rise of #LadybugMakeup highlights whimsical, insect-inspired makeup looks also tailored to spooky season. Across manicure content, #UglyNails are performing well, as more unconventional and unusual nail designs gain traction for allowing artistic expression, while #PinkCateyeNails reflects interest in light-reflecting cateye designs in shades of pink. The #CoilyCurly hashtag celebrates natural hair textures between curly and coily, with content focused on haircare tips and styling.

Products that combine hydration, targeted care and sensory experiences are ruling the bodycare category. Hydrating body mists meet demand for lightweight, water-like moisturizers that deliver lotion-level hydration, while anti-sweat hand creams offer targeted solutions for managing perspiration on the hands. Growing demand for hand mists suggest interest in convenient, fragrant formats that refresh and sanitize on the go, while niacinamide body wash is an example of products designed to support the skin’s moisture barrier. Finally, strawberry body scrub reflects demand for fruit-inspired bodycare that combines exfoliation with appealing scents and ingredients.

Across bodycare brands, there’s growing interest in those offering specialized and efficient approaches to personal care and grooming. Carpe reflects demand for clinical-strength sweat and odor control, while Hanni highlights simplified bodycare through “skip-step” essentials, with a particular rise in searches for its Splash Salve in-shower body balm. Proraso stands out for its Italian men’s grooming heritage. Estée Lauder has evolved its fragrance range by incorporating bodycare into its iconic scent collections, as searches for its Beautiful Perfumed Body Powder grow. Meanwhile, Prequel reflects interest in dermatologist-developed, science-backed skincare centered on skin barrier health.

This week on TikTok, the #DiscountMakeup hashtag is flooded with shoppers unexpectedly discovering Jeffree Star Cosmetics products at Dollar Tree. Meanwhile, content around #PerfumeMists is focused on reviews and recommendations of lightweight, refreshing fragrance formats. #TattooLipLiner content is also on the rise, featuring ink-like liners, peel-off stains, and semi-permanent lip treatments for long-lasting lip definition. #GlowyMakeupRoutine points to interest in luminous, radiant makeup looks and routines, while #FeatheredHair highlights interest in the ’70s voluminous, heavily layered hair look. Together, these trends highlight how beauty content is increasingly shaped by product discovery, makeup routines and nostalgic aesthetics.

There’s growing interest in fragrance trends that combine personalization, identity, and convenience. Alcohol-free fragrances, for example, reflect demand for alternative formulations to traditional perfumes, while custom perfumes point to interest in personalized scents tailored to individual preferences. The rise of masculine fragrances suggests that scent is increasingly functioning as an identity marker for male and female consumers alike, while gothic perfume reflects demand for darker and more mysterious aromatic profiles that evoke the romantic and atmospheric elements of the goth aesthetic. Finally, travel fragrances, the portable and convenient scent formats designed to make fragrance easier to pack and use on the go, are also trending.

This month, there’s particular interest in fragrance brands offering distinctive approaches to scent. Lore’s emotive, transportive fragrances translate specific moods and places into immersive scent experiences, while MCM Fragrance and Miu Miu highlight growing interest in luxury scents that extend recognizable fashion identities into fragrance, with searches for the latter mainly associated with Miutine and its youthful fragrance identity. Ranger Station stands out for its bold, high-concentration, nature-inspired scents, while Maison d’Etto offers perfumes rooted in equestrian influence, contemporary art and architecture. These brands highlight growing consumer interest in fragrance that goes beyond scent itself, offering distinctive stories, identities and sensory experiences.

As we enter October season, #SpookyNailArt is trending on TikTok, reflecting interest in Halloween-inspired nail designs based on playful motifs. Meanwhile, growing interest in the #MakeupColorTheory reinforces the rise of consumers learning about the hues that enhance their features. #ConcertHair highlights demand for hairstyles that are durable, creative and highly accessorized, specifically designed to last throughout a concert, while the #RomanticUpdo reflects interest in soft, feminine hairstyles and intentionally undone styles. #CologneHaul shows interest in discovering and showcasing fragrance purchases and collections.

When it comes to nails, there’s a growing interest in trends that combine precision, personalization, and visually distinct finishes. The Italian manicure, which creates the appearance of longer slender nails, reflects demand for more precise techniques, while nail art pens and letters on nails point to interest in customized designs and intricate details. The rise of glass nail polish highlights a preference for glossy, translucent finishes, and vibrant nails reflect demand for bold, eye-catching colors.

Among this month’s trending nail brands, there’s a clear preference for distinct approaches to at-home manicures. Reusable, press-on nail line Never Have I Ever incorporates licensed artwork from independent artists and cultural icons into nail designs, while Double Rhythm reinforces interest in accessible, soak-off gel polishes and nail art supplies for DIY and salon-style looks. IPolish stands out for its digital color-changing press-on nails, allowing users to switch between hundreds of shades using a smartphone and activation wand. Heyhae offers sun-cured gel nail strips that harden naturally in sunlight without requiring a traditional UV or LED lamp, while Sparkle & Co. specializes in DIY dip powders with unique glitters, foils, flakes, glow-in-the-dark, and color-changing effects.

TikTok is seeing an influx of content featuring #BumperBangs, reflecting interest in vintage 1940s and ’50s fringe styles consisting of a bold, rounded shape. Meanwhile, the rise of #CurlyHairBride highlights demand for bridal hair inspiration that embraces natural curls and textured styles. #WigsOnTikTok shows the growing role of TikTok in discovering, styling, and showcasing wigs. #UltaFragrance and #SephoraBeautyAdvisor highlight interest in beauty advisors sharing recommendations, product expertise and customer interactions at retailers Ulta and Sephora. Together, these hashtags highlight interest in vintage looks, occasion-specific styling, and behind-the-scenes beauty retail experiences.

There’s a growing interest in makeup products that combine ease of use, enhanced appearance, and convenient beauty benefits, according to monthly search data. Growth in creamy lip liners points to demand for smooth, easy-to-apply products that shape and define the lips, while lip volumizers help create the appearance of fuller, smoother lips without invasive treatments. Rose gold eyeshadow is also trending, driven by demand for warm, luminous shades. Gripping primer, which is a gel-based product with a tacky finish to hold your makeup in place, reflects interest in creating durable makeup looks that last throughout the day. The rise of SPF face powder reveals interest in facial sun protection beyond conventional sunscreens, with multifunctional products that both protect and control shine.

Across makeup brands, those offering distinctive products spanning various price points are performing particularly well. Hung Vanngo Beauty reflects demand for makeup artist expertise, while Burberry Beauty signals continued interest in luxury cosmetics from established fashion houses. C-beauty brand Cheeryep and Sleek Makeup highlight demand for vibrant, high-pigment makeup and innovative finishes. Maven Beauty, Fashion Nova’s makeup brand, suggests growing demand for affordable beauty options.

On TikTok, #UVHairExtensions are gaining traction, reflecting interest in innovative UV and LED hair extension techniques offering fast application, while #BrownRedHair highlights demand for rich, warm hair color combinations of brown, red, copper, and mahogany tones. Manicurist content featuring #PracticeNails shows past designs and their training progress, while #CottagecoreNails spotlights whimsical, nature-inspired manicures influenced by cottagecore aesthetics. The rise of #BridesmaidsMakeup reflects growing demand for beauty inspiration tailored to bridesmaids and wedding looks.

In skincare, monthly interest in products and treatments that combine targeted skin health benefits with gentle, barrier-supporting ingredients and advanced technologies is rising. Silicone-free sunscreen and its lightweight, ingredient-conscious sun protection is trending, while the retinol sandwich method, where retinol is layered between moisturizer to reduce the risk of irritation, is gaining traction among those looking to safely introduce retinol into their routines. There is continued demand for hyaluronic acid face lotions offering convenient, hydrating properties that support moisture retention and skin plumpness, while ceramide toners are designed to strengthen and maintain the skin barrier. Interest in high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) treatments highlights demand for advanced, non-invasive aesthetic treatments focused on skin tightening and rejuvenation.
