#6702. The 22 Best European Christmas Markets to Visit This Winter

There’s nothing quite like a Christmas market to set a joyful tone for the holiday season. Is there anywhere else where it’s acceptable to mill about with a hearty mug of glögg in one hand, an even larger potato pancake in the other, while exceeding your budget on handcrafted ornaments and posing for photos in front of a wooden sleigh? The answer, we can confidently say, is no.

If you’re especially fortunate, you might even find yourself exploring a traditional European Christmas market this winter—a bucket list item for travelers with a proclivity for all things merry and bright. A natural place to start when curating an itinerary is Germany, and for good reason: It is, after all, the birthplace of the Christmas market, with Dresden’s Striezelmarkt first springing up all the way back in 1434.

But it’s hardly the only country that excels at this holiday event. There are numerous other destinations scattered across the continent—some familiar, and some wonderfully under the radar—that deliver the festive goods. Here, find 22 storybook European Christmas markets to make 2026 your most memorable holiday season yet.

What to Expect: The Stortorget Christmas Market is held in Gamla Stan, Stockholm’s old town, that dates back to the 13th century and is encircled by historic merchant houses. It’s often snowy this time of year, so enjoy the crunch of fresh powder beneath your feet as you meander medieval alleys and peruse the market’s 41 chalet-shaped stalls. If you’re hungry, pick up a smoked sausage or some lussekatter, a brioche-like saffron bun. You can cross everyone off your shopping list with the cozy selection of hand-knitted sweaters and traditional ornaments, all illuminated by the market’s endless strings of festive lights. (And speaking of light, if your visit to Stockholm happens to land on December 13, don’t miss Lucia, the country’s traditional, candlelit festival.)

Where to Stay: Lydmar Hotel (12-minute walk)

What to Expect: The term ‘fairytale’ gets thrown around a lot when speaking of Christmas markets, but in the case of Wroclaw, it’s simply the best way to describe it. This magical atmosphere—complete with gothic architecture and a 75-foot-tall (artificial!) Norwegian spruce—stretches across four interconnected areas: the market square (Rynek), the salt square (Plac Solny), Świdnicka Street, and Oławska Street. While exploring, don’t miss the opportunity to try oscypek, a smoked cheese from the Polish mountains that is served with cranberries and best paired with a glass of mead (Poland’s oldest traditional alcoholic drink).

Where to Stay: Hotel Altus Palace (15-minute walk)

Location: Place des Dominicains, Place Jeanne d’Arc, Place de l’Ancienne Douanne, Koïfhus, Place des Six Montagnes Noires, and Square de la Montagne Verte.

When: Ends December 29 (though the Gourmet Market runs until January 3)

What to Expect: There are six (yes, six) total markets in this little town, which looks like the missing chapter of a fairytale book even when it’s not covered in string lights and fir branches. They’re all scattered around the Old Town and serve slightly different purposes: The main one on Place des Dominicains is mostly arts and crafts themed, with a few kids’ rides spread; the Place Jeanne d’Arc market is set up to look like a traditional Alsatian village; the Marché Gourmand at Square de la Montagne Verte is the spot for scrapings of creamy raclette, rich tartiflette, and hot cups of mulled wine.

Where to Stay: Relais & Châteaux La Maison Des Têtes (3-minute walk)

What to Expect: Dating back to the 17th century, the Nuremberg Christmas market (“Christkindlesmarkt”) is one of the first on the continent, and the city certainly goes all-out in homage to this tradition. Nicknamed the “city of wood and cloth,” it stands out for its candy cane-striped cloth tents, each housing glass tree baubles, fresh-baked gingerbread, and handmade wooden trinkets. Traveling with little ones? The children’s Christmas market is just around the corner on Hans-Sachs-Platz, and includes everything from a lit-up merry-go-round to a bake house where they can roll out their own dough.

Where to Stay: Karl August (one-minute walk)

Location: On Barfüsserplatz and Münsterplatz in the historic old town.

What to Expect: In Basel, around 155 rustic wooden chalets are set against the backdrop of the city’s old town, set aglow with glittering lights. A magnificent Christmas tree is erected in the historic center with ornaments by local decorating legend Johann Wanner, while stalls are bedecked in string lights and tinsel at every turn. After picking up a few artisanal gifts and goodies, head for the 13-meter-high Christmas pyramid on Barfüsserplatz for mulled wine, followed by a stroll along the Rhine River.

Where to Stay: Les Trois Rois (10-minute walk)

What to Expect: The Wiener Chriskindlemarkt und Weihnachtstraum Christmas market is perhaps the largest and well-known in Vienna, but with this precedent comes crowds. Instead, founder of bespoke travel company Black Tomato Tom Marchant points to the Christmas village at the Belvedere Palace as an in-the-know, less-trafficked alternative preferred by locals; here, you can wander around the palace’s lavish 18th-century Baroque architecture while indulging in mulled wine and delectable pastries. “Lots of locally crafted jewelry can be found in this area,” says Marchant. “Scented woods, ceramics, wooden hats, decorations, drinking horns—it’s quite a stunning place.”

Where to Stay: Miiro Spittelberg (20 minutes by tram)

What to Expect: Known by holiday devotees as the “capital of Christmas,” Strasbourg is home to the oldest holiday market in France, dating all the way back to 1570. Visitors to this picturesque city in the Alsace region can pop in and out of 13 quaint markets, all within walking distance of each other in the old town. The original, however, is known as Christkindelsmärik and can be found at Place Broglie—there you, can sip on a mug of vin chaud while zipping around tinsel-adorned chalets in front of the Gothic cathedral.

Where to Stay: Hotel Cour du Corbeau Strasbourg-Mgallery (15-minute walk)

What to Expect: Christmas markets and Germany are inextricably linked—it’s been estimated that there are over 2,500 in the country alone—and one of the best places to begin your exploration of the region’s holiday traditions is in the fairytale fortress town of Heidelberg. The historic city’s landscape includes the Neckar River and Odenwald Forest, while it also boasts architectural landmarks such as the Old Bridge and a prestigious 14th-century university attended by everyone from Hegel to Hannah Arendt. Heidelberg’s Christmas market is scattered throughout the illuminated storybook alleys of the old town, where the smell of roasted nuts wafts in the air as you dip into huts for souvenirs. Kids in tow? Go ice skating on Karlsplatz, or take a spin on the antique carousel.

Where to Stay: Heidelberg Suites House of Hütter (10-minute walk)

Where to Stay: Telegraaf Hotel (5-minute walk)

What to Expect: With the unmistakable silhouettes of Edinburgh Castle and the Scott Monument in the distance, Edinburgh’s holiday market—located in the center of the Scottish city—imbues its ancient walkways with a lively charm. Take in bird’s eye views from atop the glittering ferris wheel or glide across the ice skating rink surrounded by 18th-century architecture. Afterward, trot around the cheery network of vendors serving Scottish delicacies and winter drinks, or pick up last-minute artisanal gifts and decorations at the market’s many boutique stalls.

Where to Stay: The Roseate Edinburgh (10-minute drive)

Location: Tivoli Gardens and Højbro Plads

When: Ends January 3 and December 20, respectively

What to Expect: Entering Copenhagen’s Tivoli Gardens during the holiday season feels like wandering into an undiscovered Nordic village. This 175-year-old theme park is transformed annually into a Christmas market with 60 stalls swathed in magical decor, including log cabins draped in pine cones and layers of snow—and that’s without mentioning the garden itself, which glows with over 70,000 Christmas baubles and 1,000-plus trees draped in lights. A 10-minute walk away, Højbro Plads also lures in visitors with 18,000 sparkling lights, plus live reindeer pulling a Santa’s sleigh.

Where to Stay: Villa Copenhagen (5 and 15-minute walk)

What to Expect: If you’re looking for a more pastoral feel, head to the Cotswolds, England’s most romantic region of storybook countryside. “With quaint villages adorned in lights, caroling, and frequent dustings of snow, the Cotswolds evokes Christmas from the days of old,” Marchant says. The ancient city of Bath sits on the region’s edge and is hosting the 20th anniversary of its annual holiday market this year. With over 150 stalls offering unique goods like pottery, hand-knit socks, artisan cheeses, and beyond, you’ll cross off your shopping list—and then some.

Location: Govone Castle and Asti’s historic center

What to Expect: Bordering France and Switzerland, Italy’s northern Piedmont region is a hotspot for wintry festivities—but the atmospheric Christmas markets of neighboring towns Govone and Asti are the real standout. In Govone, tucked away inside the 18th-century royal castle, is both the House of Santa Claus and an exhibition that timelines the city’s Christmas celebrations over the centuries. If you want to shop, however, nearby Asti is where you’ll find over 130 workstations of artisans and food and wine producers scattered across Italy; afterwards, visit the living nativity scene put on by nearly 100 local volunteers.

Where to Stay: Relais San Maurizio (30-minute drive)

What to Expect: If you ask Finns where Santa Claus comes from, they’ll proudly declare their country as the answer. (Lapland, to be precise.) This alone makes celebrating the holiday in the capital of Helsinki an exhilarating and celebratory affair. “This is one of the best holiday markets in Europe,” Marchant says. “The cathedral overlooks the Helsinki Christmas market, which has over 100 stalls and stands with hand-crafted gifts, ornaments, locally-grown produce, and fish and meats sourced hyper-locally.” What are you waiting for?

Where to Stay: Hotel Haven (5-minute walk)

Location: Vorosmarty Square and St. Stephen’s Basilica

What to Expect: Brave the bone-chilling weather with a bowl of goulash soup or steaming chimney cake at Budapest’s beloved Christmas market located along the cobblestone streets of Vörösmarty Tér (Vorosmarty Square) in the heart of the city. About a 10-minute walk away you can also discover Christmas festivities in front of St. Stephen’s Basilica; the advent festival hosts around 100 craft exhibitors, an ice rink, and more. (It was named Best Christmas Market in Europe for three years in a row, if that sort of accolade piques your interest.)

Where to Stay: Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest (5-minute walk)

What to Expect: This century-old holiday fair has over 100 wooden stalls and is nestled in Madrid’s Plaza Mayor town square. The merrymaking vibes are cemented with a glowing carousel, nativity scenes (belénes), and loads of handcrafted ornaments and gifts to choose from. You can also savor seasonal Spanish flavors like churros con chocolate washed down with a cup of mulled wine.

Where to Stay: Rosewood Villa Magna (15-minute drive)

Location: Market Square and Simon Stevin Square

What to Expect: Appointed the whimsical title of Winter Glow, the annual festival in the medieval city of Bruges is nothing short of magical. Begin your visit on the light trail; a walk along 10 illuminated installations, all connected by a wintry blue glow. Then head for the Christmas markets for festivities that feel plucked from a fairytale. Technically there are two markets—one in the Market Square and the other in Simon Stevin Square—but as they are situated less than a five-minute walk from each other, it’s easy to do both. Peruse the atmospheric stalls for handcrafted decorations, wool socks, and plenty of Belgian treats and mulled wine, followed by a spin around the ice rink.

Where to Stay: Hotel Van Cleef (10-minute walk)

Location: Roßmarkt, along the Zeil, down to Römerberg, and to the Main River.

What to Expect: With origins dating back to the 14th century, the Frankfurt Christmas market is among the oldest in the world. As such, it’s also one of the most popular markets, attracting millions of festive guests each year and stretching across several parts of the old town. Meander through its many decorated stalls, make a pitstop at the tree in Römerberg square, and don’t forget to devour a bethmännchen (a marzipan pastry that is unique to Frankfurt and baked just for Christmas).

Where to Stay: Schlosshotel Kronberg (30-minute drive)

What to Expect: This traditional market is cozied up in the heart of Salzburg’s UNESCO World Heritage Site and has origins that go back to the late 15th century. These days, Christmas lovers descend upon the market’s 100-plus stands in search of Austrian specialties, festive incense aromas, traditional crafts, and decorations for the tree—all found within traditional huts.

Where to Stay: Rosewood Schloss Fuschl (30-minute drive)

Location: Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square

What to Expect: Soak up the magic of Czechia at Prague’s holiday market. Get into the spirit of the season as you hop from one decorated wooden hut to the next, purchasing artisan crafts and delectable treats along the way. Curious what you’ll be eating? Look to popular Czech dishes like šunka (big hams roasted on spits), klobása (barbecued sausages), and rybí polévka (a traditional Christmas soup).

Where to Stay: Four Seasons Hotel Prague (10 to 20 minute walk)

What to Expect: For those in search of something out of the ordinary, Valkenburg’s underground Christmas markets are a winning bet. The small southern Dutch town hits all the marks when it comes to setting the right tone for the season, but once you head into its caves and tunnels that’s when the magic truly begins. Bedecked in twinkly lights, these merry passages wind beneath castle ruins and offer stalls stocked with gifts and goodies. There’s even a cave with life-size sand sculptures and 3-D holiday paintings. Above ground, pay a visit to Santa’s Village, a more traditional market filled with chalets serving up hot drinks and Christmas trinkets.

Where to Stay: Château St. Gerlach (10-minute drive)

Where to Stay: Amerikalinjen (10-minute walk)

#6701. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6700. 25 Best Airbnbs in Paris 2026 for a Stylish Sojourn in the City of Light

When you book something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

There are two sorts of Parisian holidays. The first, an exercise in blissful escapism, where luxury hotels, gallery hopping, and lazy apéros à la terrasse all help you lean into the romantic undercurrent of the city. The second, an exercise in make-believe: You would not be the first person to plot a move to Paris halfway through your stay there, earmarking local boulangeries and wine shops as favorites and spending mornings chit-chatting with market vendors. If you lean toward the latter experience, this is where the best Airbnbs in Paris enter the picture. After all, what better way to cosplay a Parisienne than via a cozy flat of your own (albeit a temporary one)?

Our edit is an evolving one—there’s no shortage of stately Haussmann buildings available for rent—grouped by arrondissement. (There are 20 total, and while we haven’t hit on all of them, the below list includes several of the most popular for visitors.) Each spot has its own distinct flair, depending on what sort of Parisian you wish to embody. The chichi traveler with high-brow tastes will love the classic charm of the Left Bank; the arty fashion-lover will prefer the cozy studios of the Marais (as well as its proximity to some of the best vintage shops); the low-key bohemian will find respite in the hills of Montmarte, above the city’s lights. Grand architecture and bistro balconies, you’ll be glad to discover, have no loyalty to any particular arrondissement. They’re all good; you really can’t go wrong.

For anyone planning a trip to the City of Light, consider the roundup of properties ahead for a true immersive experience in one of the most stylish cities on the planet.

For a grand apartment right in the middle of the historical center, book this ornate Airbnb. Travelers looking to see all the sights will appreciate its proximity to the Palais Royal, Centre Pompidou, and the Louvre; it’s also around the corner from the Les Halles shopping center, where you’ll find both great restaurants (Le Petit Bouillon Pharamond is a nice option for an affordable lunch and gorgeous interiors) and little shops (E. Dehillerin, Julia Child’s much-frequented kitchenware store, is a must). The home itself is no less impressive—high ceilings with crown molding, antique gilded mirrors, and parquet floors run throughout.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, indoor fireplace, long-term stays allowed, elevator

Exposed beams and parquet flooring set the scene for this typically charming Parisian apartment. There’s lots of space for making yourself right at home, including a stunning balcony that sits atop Rue de Rivoli so you’ll feel like you’re right in the middle of everything as you sip your morning espresso while mapping out the day’s itinerary. Then there’s the location: If it’s your first time visiting Paris, the fact that the Louvre museum, the Centre Pompidou, and the Seine are all within walking distance will be a massive bonus. Leave the complicated commutes for your sophomore outing; this home lets you walk everywhere.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, blackout shades, Devialet Bluetooth sound system, television, air conditioning, kitchen, dishwasher, espresso machine, balcony, housekeeping available at a cost

This sun-drenched two-bedroom near the Seine opens with a grand, golden-colored lobby, complete with a spiral staircase and tile floors. Upstairs, the duplex has lots of space to stretch out, from a dining table that doubles as a workspace to a bright living room to a small balcony. You’ll have both the fifth and sixth floors—but as there’s no elevator, prepare to get your cardio in. It’s in a fun area, too; Pizzeria Popolare, a great Italian restaurant, is just down the street, and you’re within easy exploring distance of all the boutiques and galleries the Marais has to offer.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, Bluetooth sound system, television, balcony, pets allowed

Best for: A small group of friends—who still want their own space.

We’d book this Airbnb for the tiles alone. From the rainbow-colored bathtub to the celery green kitchen to the traditional tomettes that run throughout, it’s an effortlessly charming spot, located on the third floor of an 18th-century building. The enviable design continues from the baby blue bedroom to the painted furniture; it’ll be more than obvious that you’re staying in one of the more creative, artistic quartiers of the city. (And if you want to get some of your own work done, the dedicated office area is happy to oblige.) While it’s in a bustling neighborhood, the apartment itself is at the back of the property, so you’ll have quiet when you need it.

If you picked the Marais because of its art scene, you might as well commit to the experience and book an Airbnb directly overlooking the Picasso Museum. (Plus you’re just five minutes from Berthillon, the best ice cream in the area.) The second thing, of course, is its style. Even the piano area, a tiny nook off one of the bedrooms, has a blue marble floor and matching tile mural—it’s all extremely decadent.

We found your Parisian tree house. A bedroom adorned in pink toile de Jouy print, a working fireplace in the living room, a dining room that’s overflowing with plants and dressed up with a gilded mirror: this apartment, to borrow some first-level French, is très chic. Steps away from the bustling Odéon neighborhood and landmarks like the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden, this apartment is ideally situated for first-timers to the city of lights. With original 1930s features preserved and played up, it's also well-decorated: Art Deco details, like geometric borders, curved ceiling cut-outs, and arched doorways pop up throughout. (The turquoise bathtub nook is a particular highlight; the glass wall in the dining room is another.) This rental has tons of space for a family as well as several kid-friendly amenities available upon request; book it for a longer stay in the city.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, piano, Bluetooth sound system, exercise equipment, television, high chair, board games, elevator, parking, pets allowed

Location: By the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden

This literary, light-filled Airbnb is located in a building that houses several artists studios—notes of which can be found everywhere from the airy, industrial-style layout to the perfectly imperfect collection of decor to the multi-colored tiles in the kitchen. (As for the literary tie-in: Bookworms will appreciate the massive wall of books in the upstairs bedroom. Take your pick.) The home is mere blocks away from the Jardin du Luxembourg, in Montparnasse. Browse the aforementioned bookshelf and grab a paperback, pick up a coffee from one of the many cafés in the area, and take a morning to yourself in the gardens.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer/dryer, TV, crib, courtyard

Best for: Avid readers always looking for a new, picturesque spot to get lost in a book.

For the solo traveler who never wants to be too far from the sparkling lights of the Eiffel Tower, this little studio is a cozy cocoon just six minutes away. (Starting quite literally with the bed, which is cordoned off from the rest of the space by a chic glass wall and a gauzey curtain.) A tiny kitchenette stocked with all the essential appliances lets you make the most of local treats—helpful, as the famous Rue Cler street market is just around the corner, so you can stock up on cheeses, quiche, and even rotisserie chickens for quiet meals at home.

Amenities: Washer, elevator, pet-friendly, housekeeping available at a fee

Location: On Rue Amélie, a quick walk to the Eiffel Tower

It’ll be hard to beat this central location: This sunny, spacious two-bedroom is situated directly at the base of the Champ de Mars, the grassy park that houses the Eiffel Tower. It’s as stately as its zip code implies—think, period-appropriate wall moldings that reflect its 19th-century origins and oversized windows, with the occasional unexpected pop of color (like a yellow window in the kitchen and pistachio dining chairs) to keep it from feeling stuffy. It also comes with an espresso machine, so if you ever tire of your local boulangerie—unlikely—you can start the day with coffee at home.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3

Location: At the foot of the Eiffel Tower

Best for: Ticking the Eiffel Tower off your bucket list.

It’s conveniently located in the heart of Paris and stocked with modern creature comforts like a Nespresso machine and a Netflix-enabled television, but you really only need one reason to book this apartment: the massive terrace. Equipped with outdoor dining and seating, it’s a rare thing to find in the busy city (and, should you ever want a little quiet, an ideal spot to enjoy an apéro at home). Though it only has one proper bedroom, it can actually sleep four thanks to a sofa bed in the living room. For families looking for a comfortable spot near all the top sights, this is a great option.

Amenities: Washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Bose sound system, exercise equipment, travel crib, kitchen, Nespresso coffee maker, dishwasher, terrace, paid parking available

Best for: Travelers for whom a terrace with a view is a non-negotiable.

Staying in this palatial sixth-floor penthouse will feel like time travel—it sits within a historic Haussmann building and offers original details like 18th-century wood floors, hand-painted wallpaper, antique fireplaces, and a Napoleon-style oval room. It’s bourgeois luxury in every sense. The entire space enjoys plenty of light thanks to French windows opening onto three balconies, and amenities like a full kitchen and entry hall with a piano will make it difficult to venture outside (though you’ll want to—it’s in close proximity to some of Paris’s most coveted attractions like the Louvre, Opera Garnier, Champs Élysées).

Amenities: Washer/dryer, piano, kitchen, elevator, balcony, antique fireplaces

Best for: Anyone who knows what a “Napoleon-style oval room” is (interior design buffs, this one’s for you).

On the fifth floor of a traditional Haussmann building (there is an elevator, don’t worry) sits this elegant sunny spot. A long balcony stretches outside and includes a small bistro set for breakfasts outside—though the spacious dining room is also an enticing option. From the red-and-cream checkerboard kitchen to the ornate crown molding in the living area, it’s endlessly charming. Montmartre is only 15 minutes away; perhaps more importantly, depending on what your itinerary priorities are, the famous bakery Mamiche is an even-shorter 10 minute walk. (The brioche and the ham sandwich alone are good reasons to make a daily pilgrimage there each morning.)

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, sound system, board games, fire place, balcony, elevator

Best for: Design inspiration and proximity to an incredible bakery.

Originally belonging to the painter Georges Braque back in 1911, this sweet studio has since been re-done and can now fit up to four guests (the sofa converts to a bed, if you don’t mind a slightly crowded living space). The renovation didn’t strip it of its character, though, and between the primary-colored kitchen storage cubbies and the floor-to-ceiling windows that let the light stream in, it’s one of the more unique apartment rentals in Paris. The bay windows look out onto a courtyard, so you’ll have plenty of peace despite being located in one of the city’s most bustling areas for nightlife.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, kitchen, shared backyard, coffee maker, crib/travel crib/children’s books available upon request, balcony

Best for: Those hoping to experience the city’s artistic spirit beyond a visit to the Louvre.

Right below Pigalle on Rue Cadet, this quiet one-bedroom is surrounded by bakeries, cheese shops, and greengrocers. Everything you’d need is within walking distance; head to Racines, a hole-in-the-wall Italian spot with a decadent tiramisù, for a date night in the neighborhood. Inside, a fully equipped kitchen and multiple workspaces ensure you have all the essentials to stretch out and make this temporary spot feel like home. With sloping ceilings and views onto the city’s greyscale rooftops, it feels like the coziest attic—peaceful, personal, and chic enough to make you want to stay awhile.

Amenities: Washer, kitchen, dishwasher, coffee maker

If you can’t pick between the trendy 10th or 3rd arrondissements—don’t. This bright and airy one-bedroom is smack in the middle, in an ideal area full of hole-in-the-wall eateries and stylish spots to grab an apéro before a late dinner. Since it’s owned and designed by an architect, its interiors are especially appealing: The blend of vintage furniture and flourishing greenery might just inspire you to redecorate when you get home. In the meantime, you’ll feel right at home. The kitchen is big enough to whip up meals of your own, if you feel inspired—or at least, a quick breakfast before heading out for the day.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 2

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Apple sound system, piano, kitchen, dishwasher, Nespresso coffee maker

Location: Right on the border of the 10th and the 3rd arrondissements

Best for: Bookmarking design inspiration.

Overlooking the rooftops of Paris, this small but well-appointed apartment (yes, it has an elevator) is perfect for a couple. From a zellige-tiled kitchen to a teeny balcony where you can sip a cocktail during golden hour, you’ll find everything you need for a short stint in the city. But the best part is, hands down, its location: The home is right by the Canal. Here, you’ll find a livelier, younger scene, with natural wine bars, trendy restaurants, and an atmosphere that feels decidedly removed from the touristy center. (Early June, a local-favorite restaurant and wine bar with a rotating cast of guest chefs, is a leisurely 15-minute walk away.)

Best for: Proximity to your new favorite wine bar.

For a vacation rental that feels designed by someone’s French grandma, choose this colorful, eclectic spot and make yourself at home. The kitchen, with its checkerboard-covered table, citron walls, and collected jumble of various tools and trinkets, is undoubtedly the center; but the bedrooms (there are three), with their massive windows and original terracotta floors are also nice—especially if you’re traveling with a big group, and want to make sure you each have enough space. When you do want to dine out, you’ll be well-positioned: Bistrot des Tournelles and Chez Paul, two wonderful traditional bistros, are located in this neighborhood.

Best for: Cosplaying Julia Child for the weekend.

Not all Parisian Airbnbs involve ornate crown moldings and baroque antiques; some, like this loft, can lean quite industrial. Iron beams and high ceilings make it seem even more spacious (the space itself is located in an old printing house); glass windows overlook an internal courtyard, if you need a quiet temporary home. Sandwiched between République and Canal St. Martin, it’s in a fun, more local part of the city. If it’s warm enough, walk along the water in the afternoon before ducking into Chambre Noir, a little wine bar near the apartment, for small plates and a crisp glass of white.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, TV, air conditioning, pet-friendly

Best for: Fans of industrial architecture.

This two-bedroom apartment may just house the best balcony in all of Paris. It’s well-furnished, with plenty of potted plants and a bistro set for taking your breakfast outside, weather-permitting, but the views of the Haussmann buildings and Eiffel Tower in the distance are what makes it really special. Inside, the design is cozy, with floral quilts and Art Deco-inspired lighting casting everything in a warm glow. Even the entrance to the apartment is special. While the fifth floor rental is accessible by elevator, you may just find yourself choosing to take the stairs, which are lined with stained glass windows.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, Sonos Bluetooth sound system, indoor fireplace, air conditioning, coffee maker, balcony, outdoor furniture, elevator

Perched in the heart of Montmartre in the hilly, cobblestone-lined streets of the Abbesses neighborhood, this one-bedroom home is ideal for the couple who likes their decor collected, full of personality, and a tiny bit mismatched. Starting with the mix of antique furnishings in the living room (including a red velvet armchair) and going right through to the lemon-yellow bedroom, the design of this place will make you feel like you’re visiting your artistic Parisian friend—no cold, white-box rooms here. When you do want to hit the tourist spots, the Basilica of Sacré Coeur is just a 15-minute walk away.

Best for: The eclectic traveler coming to Paris to peruse the flea markets.

You’re alone in Paris, and you need an inspiring studio from which to focus on your creative project (or just finish your book in peace): This artist’s loft is it. Tall ceilings and an oversized window create a light-filled environment, while a dedicated workspace offers a quiet place to concentrate. There’s a small but well-appointed kitchen so you can cook your meals at home and truly feel at ease during your stay, however long it may be.

Amenities: Washer, crib, coffee maker, shared backyard

Best for: Anyone coming to Paris to get out of a creative rut.

From the terracotta tomettes to the oversized windows, this sunny one-bedroom is perfect for the solo traveler or a couple. The building dates back to the 19th century, but the decor is firmly 21st: Butter yellow bedding and a mustard-striped kitchen skirt are design ideas to bookmark for when you get home. And you can’t trump the location: It’s right in the heart of Montmartre, only a few blocks away from Boulangerie Raphaëlle (one of the all-time best bakeries in the city—trust us).

Amenities: Travel crib available upon request, coffee maker

Jeans and ballerinas are the unofficial uniform of the city (and, conveniently, make a comfortable ensemble for a day of shopping). Bring an extra-large tote as your personal item on the plane so you have plenty of space to shuttle back all your souvenirs… including some French pharmacy goodies, of course.

After combing through hundreds of listings in a destination’s most desirable neighborhoods, we narrow down our list by reviewing a variety of determining factors, from the logistics of price, location, and amenities, to important details such as reviews and host information. From there, we take into consideration aesthetic details such as design, natural light, and overall look and feel of the home. The final edit is a well-rounded list that ensures booking a stay will result in a safe and stylish holiday.

#6699. Behind the Scenes of the Inaugural Bon Appétit LIVE

This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.

The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just launched a new cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.

Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.

In the first class of the day, baking novices and aficionados alike joined senior Test Kitchen editor and BA Bake Club expert Jesse Szewczyk in the Test Kitchen for Pie Crust Fundamentals, presented by East Fork. The hands-on class featured guest Keia Mastrianni, brand storyteller and “unofficial pie lady” of East Fork. Mastrianni proclaimed her enthusiasm for pie making: “I love preaching the gospel of pie. My favorite thing is teaching people to make pie dough with their hands.” Szewczyk agreed, emphasizing the tactile nature of the process: “It’s a very physical thing to do…a recipe can be written, but teaching someone to make pie dough requires demonstration.” Participants were in luck as Szewczyk and Mastrianni demonstrated a buttery pie crust fortified with cream cheese, a recipe ideal for Thanksgiving developed by former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic. After Mastrianni shared crimping tips, participants made their own pie dough at stations throughout the kitchen, with Test Kitchen editors on hand to offer guidance. One participant, James, was particularly excited to be working with director of cooking Emma Laperruque. He enthused, “Before Emma’s and Chris [Morocco’s] recipes, I would burn water. [Bon Appétit] has made cooking really accessible, and I built a lot of confidence. I love the simplicity of Emma’s recipes…they are all so flavorful and so good.”

Each guest left ready for holiday baking season with new pie-making skills, and a ceramic pie dish from East Fork’s new bakeware collection, featuring clay and glaze made in-house with materials sourced in the Southeast. Before moving on to their next experience, Mastrianni encouraged everyone to keep honing their skills, emphasizing, “Practice makes pie. Progress, not perfection.”

Meanwhile, in the neighboring Demo Kitchen, a Pasta Boot Camp was underway with Bon Appétit senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman and chef Stefano Secchi. Secchi, chef and partner of New York City’s Rezdôra (recipient of one Michelin star) and Massara, honed his craft in Modena, Italy, under legendary chef Massimo Bottura.

After walking guests through the fundamentals of making and shaping fresh pasta by hand, Secchi demonstrated a filled ravioli dish aptly named Holiday in Parma. Made with 00 flour and egg dough, the ravioli was piped with a chestnut and Parmesan filling and served with a rich reduction of chicken broth, butter, and saba (a traditional Italian syrup made from slowly simmered grape must).

While guests savored their pasta in the Demo Kitchen, a lively panel discussion was underway on the 34th floor. Moderated by editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, the Bringing Culture to Cooking panel featured chefs Fariyal Abdullahi (executive chef, Hav & Mar, NYC), Nicholas Bazik (chef and owner, Provenance, Philadelphia, a Bon Appétit Best New Restaurant of 2025), and Vijay Kumar (executive chef and partner, Semma, NYC, a Best New Restaurant of 2022). The conversation explored how culture, identity, and personal experience inform each chef’s cooking. The chefs shared some of their favorite home-cooking ingredients, such as Chef Bazik’s fermented lime juice, a versatile seasoning made by combining fresh lime juice with salt at a 2% ratio by weight. Chef Abdullahi championed berbere, the Ethiopian spice blend she likened to “Ethiopian salt” for its ubiquity in the country’s cooking. Abdullahi cautioned that store-bought blends are convenient but not necessarily of the highest-possible quality. “You should make it at home!” she encouraged.

Back in the Test Kitchen, Visit Maine hosted Lobster 101, a hands-on lobster class and oyster tasting with Bon Appétit’s manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Each participant received a whole, steamed Maine lobster and the ingredients and tools needed to transform it into a creamy, decadent lobster dip. Under Westerfield’s guidance, the class learned how to break down their lobsters, extract the meat, and assemble a dip made with cream cheese, mayonnaise, celery, chives, and lemon juice. The approachable demonstration demystified the process and showed guests how easily they could prepare a luxurious appetizer at home, just in time for the holidays.

Participants worked with hard-shell lobsters, but Tripp encouraged them to visit Maine and sample both hard-shell and soft-shell varieties. She explained that soft-shell lobsters, typically in season from July through August, have a sweeter, more tender meat. The two are actually the same animal at different stages of its molting cycle: a soft-shell lobster has recently shed its old shell, leaving a newer, more pliable one that is easier to crack. The class concluded with a tasting of Aphrodite Oysters, grown in the waters off South Thomaston, Maine. The medium-size oysters were briny and subtly sweet, reflecting the cold, brackish waters of the Lower Weskeag River where they were grown. A small squeeze of lemon was all that was needed to enhance their flavor as guests tilted their heads back, slurped, and allowed themselves to be transported to the rugged coast of Maine.

Meanwhile, in the Demo Kitchen, Bon Appétit director of culture Joseph Hernandez was joined by Matt Conroy, chef at Washington, DC’s Maison Bar à Vins, for a live cooking demonstration of one of Chef Conroy’s favorite dishes. Named one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026, the restaurant pairs French-inspired cooking with an eclectic wine list and seasonal cocktails. Chef Conroy prepared a new fall salad made of chicory, pear, and smoked blue cheese, finished with a Banyuls vinaigrette.

In the cafeteria, guests gathered for a live version of the Dear Bon Appétit advice column. Bon Appétit director of cooking Emma Laperruque presented questions about home cooking and holiday entertaining to chef Amanda Freitag. One attendee asked Freitag how to handle undercooked turkey legs and thighs each year. Freitag recommended removing the legs and cooking them separately, as in this BA recipe for Gravy-Braised Turkey from Jesse Szewczyk.

Next, food stylist Thu Buser showcased her exceptional culinary artistry by decorating an elaborate “snake cake” with vibrant green swirls and flowers. Then, a break for lunch with BA’s Best Mozzarella Sticks, a variety of salads and skewers, hot honey salmon, smoothies, and a cranberry maple mule.

While attendees grazed and mingled, Jamila Robinson joined legendary chef and restaurateur Marcus Samuelsson to discuss Back to Green: Rediscovering a World of Delicious, Healthy Eating, his new global plant-forward cookbook coauthored by Robinson. Samuelsson captured the atmosphere of the event, remarking, “What a party we are having here…the energy is amazing!”

The final demonstration of the day featured Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote presented by Visit Maine with Jesse Szewczyk and Ron Howard of Brodis Blueberries. Featuring a recipe from Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firsker, the shortcakes showcased farm-fresh wild blueberries grown on a ninth-generation family farm. As Szewczyk prepared the recipe, Howard discussed the importance of wild blueberries to Maine’s agricultural heritage. A native crop, they can be traced back to the end of the last Ice Age, predating lobster as a symbol of the state. “Everyone should think of wild blueberries as the ultimate Maine crop,” Howard explained. After tasting the shortcakes, attendees would be hard-pressed to disagree. Szewczyk noted that compared with conventional blueberries, the wild blueberries produced a more saturated color and tasted more distinctly of blueberry.

The day ended on a sweet note with pastry chef Eunji Lee, winner of North America’s Best Pastry Chef Award from The 50. Attendees had a chance to meet Lee and sample pastries from Lysée, her pastry boutique influenced by Korean and French culture and inspired by New York City.

Bon Appétit Live brought together chefs, culinary personalities, and food editors for a day of conversations, cooking, tasting, and learning. Attendees experienced the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen firsthand, learned directly from chefs and editors, and engaged with the people and products behind the food. As editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson said, “Food is always an invitation…we are so happy to give everyone access to the same experiences we have.”

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

#6697. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6695. Cranberry Brie Pull-Apart Bread

This cranberry brie pull-apart bread makes my mouth water just looking at it, and I promise your guests will feel the exact same way when you serve it at Thanksgiving Start your dinner off with a bang with this star of a holiday appetizer.

We gave our classic cheesy garlic pull-apart bread a holiday upgrade by adding beloved brie, cranberry sauce, and fresh herbs. It will not only stun on your holiday table, but will keep your guests coming back for pull after pull (after pull!) of this sweet and cheesy bread. We used a can of cranberry sauce in this recipe, but if you have some extra homemade cranberry sauce for your holiday meal (or are using up Thanksgiving leftovers), it would work perfectly here. When crosshatching the bread, slice as far down as you can without actually slicing through the bottom—you’ll have a way easier time stuffing the ingredients inside.

#6694. The Full Supermoon in Gemini Is Coming—Here’s What It Means for Every Star Sign

The last Full Moon of the season is an event we’ll reflect on for weeks as winter officially begins. Mark your calendars for December 24 at 9:53 a.m. Eastern Time to watch it peak and brighten the sky. The culmination of the monthly lunar cycle is a chance to illuminate truths and gain clarity in the darkness. A supermoon occurs when the Moon reaches perigee, its closest point to Earth. Its proximity enhances the view, making it appear larger and more luminous than usual. It is a striking, magical sight—so take a moment to soak it up.

Psychological astrologer Dr. Jennifer Freed says that this chatty, inquisitive supermoon presents a “platinum opportunity to upgrade our mindset and philosophy of life.” Freed explains: “Themes to consider: Increase networking opportunities, change negative narratives to optimal challenges, access perennial philosophies, focus on unity, speak about innovative paradigm shifts. Humor and wit are highly advised,” adding, “In general, use the quicksilver of Gemini ruled by Mercury to bring more levity and ingenuity to yourself and others.”

The Full Moon interacts with radical Uranus retrograde in Gemini, escapist Neptune retrograde in Aries, and shrewd Pluto in Aquarius. Because these generational planets move slowly, we experience their shifts as a slow burn rather than a single jolt—expect highs and lows, with a few curveballs thrown in between. There is no certainty in how matters will unfold, which is why staying receptive to new possibilities is key.

Because this Full Moon falls in Gemini, its planetary ruler is Mercury. Even though Mercury’s post-retrograde shadow (or retroshade) officially wrapped on November 30, we are still integrating the lingering aftermath of its recent backspin in Scorpio from October 24 to November 13. Be prepared for unexpected information to surface as those loose ends tie up. Any revelations may feel jarring, serving as a timely reminder to be discerning with our secrets and careful about whom we confide in.

Your words carry weight; what you articulate has a way of coming to fruition, which is why you should state your opinions, yearnings, and desires with genuine intention. Setting them free with care allows your visions to take tangible shape. Speak or journal with honesty and warmth, Aries—soon enough, you’ll see your intentions materialize in real time.

Money. Power. Fame. These three ambitions fuel your drive to realize your goals. This lunation opens up an opportunity to take the bull by the horns—provided you are ready to step into recognition and abundance. It is a moment ripe for wish fulfillment, so let your core purpose guide you toward the success you’ve been working toward.

Take a good look in the mirror. Do you appreciate the person staring back at you? The answer should be a resounding yes. If you’ve been constantly hustling toward the next milestone without taking a breather, this Full Moon is calling you to step back and find solace within yourself. Whether that means booking a spa afternoon or putting your texts on pause, make rest your top priority. Quiet restoration is essential right now.

Nothing is more fulfilling than showing up as a pillar of your community. Through collective action, you can give back meaningfully by volunteering and paying it forward. Whether contributing locally or supporting a broader cause, your generosity inspires others to follow suit without expecting anything in return. That genuine spirit is your true flex.

A promotion or leadership role you’ve been eyeing—one that previously felt out of reach—is coming back into view. Before you submit your application or bring it up with management, ground yourself in the reality of your track record so you walk in knowing your worth. The world feels expansive right now; you aren’t meant to stay confined to one single lane or location. Step out and embrace unfamiliar experiences—your travels and fresh encounters will broaden both your horizons and your convictions. Stepping outside your comfort zone will shift how you approach partnerships, freeing you from rigid ways of thinking. You are growing in real time, Libra.

Loosen your grip on control or obsessive overthinking to invite a calmer rhythm. You don’t have to meet every curveball with heavy intensity; give yourself permission to cut loose and laugh a little more often. The breath of fresh air you’ve been waiting for is finally here—take it in rather than taking it for granted.

When old social dynamics feel draining or disappointing, you naturally begin gravitating toward a fresh circle of people who genuinely share your passions. Unlike past acquaintances, these peers offer real camaraderie, a sympathetic ear, and a sounding board for your biggest ideas. You’re never truly alone with the right people in your corner—even when they're just a phone call away.

Believe it or not, there is real magic in the mundane. Channeling your energy into small, consistent habits can quietly transform your daily momentum. You don’t need a massive overhaul to hit your targets; start small by clearing your inbox promptly and editing your closet to make room for what’s next.

As one of the zodiac’s natural innovators, you are always finding inventive ways to sharpen your craft and earn recognition for your vision. Elevate your creative output by taking bolder risks in the work you share—even if it sparks debate, stepping into the cultural conversation is how you break through to the next level.

This is an ideal moment to cultivate a true sense of safety within your own sacred space, internal or physical. Letting go of lingering self-doubt and negative narratives will immediately strengthen your relationship with yourself. The sense of belonging you've been craving starts with trusting your own decisions and honoring your emotional truth.

#6693. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6692. 31 Cranberry Recipes for Thanksgiving and Beyond

Look for firm, glossy cranberries and discard any that are soft, shriveled, or bruised. A few pale pink berries are nothing to worry about.

Keep unwashed cranberries in their original bag in the refrigerator for up to four weeks, though they’re best used sooner. To stock up, freeze them in their original packaging or spread clean thoroughly dried berries on a baking sheet until frozen, then transfer to a freezer bag. They’ll keep their quality for up to a year. Many cooked cranberry recipes work with frozen berries straight from the freezer; check the recipe before thawing.

That vivid magenta filling is no food-coloring trick: Cranberries and plenty of lime give the curd its electric hue and tang. Let the pie set overnight, then pile on billowy meringue and break out the kitchen torch.

A 12-oz. bag of cranberries, sugar, orange zest, and about 10 minutes at the stove are all you need for this tangy Thanksgiving essential. Make it up to five days ahead and save any leftovers for turkey-cranberry sliders.

Layers of tender buttermilk cake, tart cranberry jam, and silky white chocolate frosting make an excellent argument for serving cake on Thanksgiving. The sugared cranberries on top are like little sour candies.

Imagine Key lime pie dressed for the holidays. The punchy cranberry-lime curd meets a crisp press-in crust made with gingersnaps and pecans. A generous dollop of whipped cream rounds out the tartness.

Here’s a reason to keep canned cranberry sauce around after Thanksgiving. Jellied sauce melts into a glossy, sweet-and-sour glaze that coats chicken and green beans. Think orange chicken, with a cranberry twist.

Cranberries turn this classic upside-down apple tart a beautiful rosy pink while cutting through its buttery sweetness. Homemade rough puff pastry supplies the flaky base; vanilla ice cream is very much encouraged.

Canned whole-berry cranberry sauce becomes a punchy dressing for pleasantly bitter endive and frisée. Add crunchy candied pecans and salty Manchego, and suddenly cranberry sauce is doing salad duty.

Two layers of buttery, crumbly walnut crust surround a tart cranberry filling in this striking take on a Linzer torte. Save it for a holiday dessert table—or any occasion that calls for something special.

Dress crisp-bottomed Persian rice with dried cranberries, saffron, and fragrant herbs. The berries plump in ghee alongside rosemary, sage, and thyme, adding little pops of sweetness against the savory rice.

If the wobble is the best part of canned cranberry sauce for you, this homemade version delivers. It’s sliceable, deeply fruity, and subtly fragrant with cardamom and bay leaves. Bring on the ridges.

Roasted brussels sprouts get a lively companion in cranberry mostarda, a sweet-tart condiment with mustard seeds, prunes, and a little brandy. Make extra mostarda: It belongs on more than just sprouts.

A warm cranberry-apple topping brings plenty of tart fruit flavor to this crowd-friendly baked oatmeal. It’s a welcome breakfast when the house is full and everyone seems to wake up hungry at once.

Rum, hard cider, cranberry juice, ginger ale, and lime make a lively batch cocktail. Cranberry-studded ice cubes do double duty, keeping glasses cold and making the punch look party-ready.

Jalapeño and lime give classic cranberry sauce a bright, spicy kick. It’s especially good alongside roasted meats or piled onto a leftover turkey sandwich when you want something with a little heat.

Forget the giant roast bird for a minute. These tender, gravy-coated turkey meatballs come with a cranberry-orange marmalade jam that stands in for traditional lingonberries. A heap of mashed potatoes completes the picture.

Fresh ginger gives this cranberry relish some zip, while golden raisins and allspice round out its tartness. Spoon it onto a cheese board or save the leftovers for French toast the next morning.

Herbs in the dredge give this crunchy fried chicken Thanksgiving energy, but the quick cranberry-mustard dipping sauce is the real holiday flourish. It’s a compelling alternative to roasting an entire turkey.

Homemade cranberry-thyme syrup, Campari, and Champagne make a sparkling cocktail that’s fruity, pleasantly bitter, and dressed for a party. Make the syrup up to two weeks ahead; the drinks come together in minutes.

Boxed stuffing mix gets a serious upgrade with aromatic vegetables, dried cranberries, and the savory drippings from crisp-skinned chicken thighs. It’s Thanksgiving-adjacent comfort food, made in one skillet any night of the week.

Roasted sweet potatoes and delicata squash get a glossy, sweet-and-sour cranberry sauce made with red wine vinegar and thyme. Make extra: The agrodolce is just as good spooned over Thanksgiving turkey.

Whole orange and a cinnamon stick give this chunky cranberry sauce its fragrant warmth. Blanching the chopped orange first keeps bitterness in check, while a little butter softens the berries’ sharp edge.

A buttery, lemony custard studded with tart cranberries gives this Southern classic a holiday spin. The berries stay mostly intact, offering juicy little bursts of tartness against the rich filling.

Dried figs bring earthy sweetness to this bold cranberry chutney, while ginger, vinegar, and whole grain mustard keep it lively. It’s the sort of condiment you’ll want beside roast pork as much as turkey.

Dorie Greenspan’s warmly spiced Bundt packs in fresh and dried cranberries, toasted almonds, and a little five-spice powder. Greek yogurt keeps the cake rich; orange icing supplies the finishing flourish.

Baker Amanda Mack tucks a tart cranberry-orange filling into exceptionally flaky buttermilk pastry for individual pies. They’re a thoughtful addition to a dessert spread where everyone wants to try a little of everything.

No simmering required for this bright, crunchy cranberry relish. Walnuts, shallot, mustard seeds, and Fresno chile give it plenty of texture and bite—a particularly good counterpoint to rich holiday mains.

Homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail its fruity punch. Lime juice keeps it lively, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim makes each glass taste decidedly more festive than a typical margarita.

Chopped fresh cranberries bring little bursts of tartness to an otherwise classic cheddar grilled cheese. A swipe of Dijon mustard ties the flavors together. Sometimes the best cranberry recipe is also lunch.

Have part of a bag left over? These ideas from the BA archives put even a small quantity to good use.

#6691. Why You Should Never Put Frozen Meat In A Slow Cooker, According To Experts

Turns out, set-it-and-forget-it has its limits.

With busy schedules and limited time each day, slow cookers are key to getting dinner on the table. They can take simple ingredients and transform them into a complete, ready-to-eat meal. Because the slow cooker does all the work for you, you may think that it can also handle defrosting meat.

But think again. The idea seems convenient in theory, but in practice, it raises some serious food safety concerns. We consulted health experts to learn more about adding frozen meat to a slow cooker. So next time you plan a hands-off dinner, you can make sure your food is delicious and safe to eat.

Sorry to be the bearer of bad news: You should never put frozen meat directly into your slow cooker. “I am all for cutting out unnecessary steps in cooking, but using frozen meat in your slow cooker is not one of them,” says Melissa Koch, RD, MEd.

Raw meat can carry harmful bacteria that cause foodborne illness. Freezing stops them from multiplying, but doesn't necessarily kill them. And because slow cookers heat food gradually, frozen meat can spend too long in what food safety experts call the “temperature danger zone.”

“The danger zone refers to a temperature range of 40°F (4°C) to 140°F (60°C) over two or more hours when harmful bacteria grow or multiply at a fast rate,” Koch explains. It can take hours for food in a slow cooker to move above the danger zone—and starting with frozen meat delays that process even further.

“The appliance heats food slowly, and starting with frozen meat means the internal temperature may sit in the ‘danger zone’ for too long,” says chef and dietitian Sharniquia White. “This gives bacteria like Salmonella or E. coli more opportunity to multiply before the food reaches a safe cooking temperature.”

What happens after eating food that has sat in the danger zone? The consequences vary based on your immune system, the extent of the contamination, and the strains of bacteria present. But none are pleasant, and some may even send you to the hospital.

“Symptoms of food-borne illness can include nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and fever,” Koch says. “You can experience the effects of food-borne illness within a few minutes to days after consuming a load of harmful pathogens or bacteria.”

Cooking frozen meat on the “low” setting of your slow cooker increases the time it spends in the danger zone, but the risk is present regardless. “The 'high' setting reduces the amount of time food spends at unsafe temperatures, but still doesn’t fully eliminate the risk when starting with frozen meat,” says White.

The ingredients you're using can also increase your risk. “Larger, denser cuts (like roasts or whole poultry) take longer to thaw and heat evenly, so they pose a greater risk of staying at unsafe temperatures for extended periods,” White explains.

Smaller pieces may thaw faster, but that doesn't necessarily make them safe to cook from frozen. White explains that ground meat is “particularly risky” because of the way it's processed, so it should be cooked thoroughly.

“I feed three young children at my home, so in my opinion, I wouldn't chance cooking frozen meat, no matter the size, in a slow cooker,” Koch says.

The answer is simple: thaw your meat before turning on your slow cooker. But your ideal method depends on how much time you have.

The safest, easiest, and least involved thawing method is to put your frozen meat in the fridge. The cold temperature of your refrigerator lets your food defrost gently without entering the danger zone.

Our editors recommend placing the meat on a plate or baking sheet to collect any juices and avoid contaminating other food in your fridge. This process can take anywhere from a couple of hours to a couple of days, depending on the cut of meat. “This requires some thought and effort, but in the long run it's worth your safety,” Koch says.

No time for that? No problem. You can thaw meat faster by submerging it in cold water in a leakproof bag, changing the water every 30 minutes, or defrosting it in the microwave, though the latter can compromise the meat's texture. Both methods require cooking the meat immediately afterward. “Once thawed, meat should go directly into the slow cooker,” White explains.

It all takes a little extra effort and planning, but it's worth it to avoid getting sick from your slow cooker dinner.

#6690. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

#6689. The Hottest Thing in Nordic Design Right Now? The Vikings

Norway is a country built on craftsmanship.

Some of the earliest, most revered pioneers of craft and international trade in the country were the Vikings, who, between the 8th and 11th centuries, used wood, iron, and bone to create their post-and-beam longhouses, weapons, and ships. (Not to mention wool, linen, and leather for their unheralded colorful attire.)

Today, as interest in Viking culture outside of Norway and Scandinavia experiences an uptick thanks to pop culture, social media, and even sports, creatives in Norway are using the opportunity to introduce a new wave of curious travelers to Viking history through artisanal clothing, metalwork, and interior design steeped in this early culture.

Traditional wool weaving at Viking Valley.

“Travelers are more interested in Viking culture than ever,” says Torill Hylland, chair of Viking Valley. Even though this Gudvangen-located recreation village debuted a decade ago, Hylland witnessed a recent surge in visitors following this past summer’s FIFA World Cup, where Norway’s Erling Haaland popularized the Viking row as one of the catchiest celebrations of the football tournament.

“We've seen significant growth in interest in Norway,” adds Nelson Oliveira, managing director, Nordics for luxury travel operator Abercrombie & Kent. Launched in 2024, their small group trip itineraries include a visit to the Viking Valley where guests interact with the Viking chieftain, dine in the reindeer-clad, candle-lit dining hall and visit the resident blacksmith, who continues to supply ironworks for the community, including door hinges and locks. “The Viking era is such an important part of Norway’s history, and we wanted to give guests an opportunity to experience that heritage beyond simply visiting a museum,” says Oliveira.

Outside the village, quotidian Viking-inspired design is flourishing—and notably predates Haaland’s viral row chant. Matilde Brandt, marketing manager of Klesarven, a Viking heritage clothing retailer founded in 2015 by Lene Lorentzen, credits the global interest in historybounding—where elements of historical fashion are incorporated into everyday styles—for the spike in popularity of their Viking-inspired styles.

“There is so much more to the [Viking] story than bearded men fighting and wearing dark colors,” says Brandt. Inspired by Hollywood’s enduringly maligned, inaccurate depictions of Viking Age Scandinavia, Klesarven focuses on historically accurate representations of the people living during that age. “Most of them were farmers, fishermen and craftspeople [who] wore bright, colorful clothing and were well put together,” says Brandt.

A Klesarven Frøya linen dress and Favn shawl.

These motifs are realized across Klesarven’s collection of wool sweaters, linen shirts, and riding skirts. One of Klesarven’s most popular designs is the Viking Age apron dress, inspired by a garment reserved for special occasions and ornamented with colorful beads, brooches, and jewelry crafted from silver, gold, and bronze. Women were also buried in these garments. “It keeps history alive,” says Brandt. “In this way, we help preserve old techniques and craftsmanship.”

Preserving heritage is also a motivation of Runestone’s founders, Sonya and Kim Andre. Having both grown up on a stretch of coastline dotted with Viking history—Sonya from Uddevalla on Sweden’s west coast and her husband, Kim, from Halden, just across the Norwegian border—Runestone was born from a personal “obsession” with Viking culture.

When the couple began building an online outfitter dedicated to Viking apparel, Norse jewelry, and rune wall art (the alphabet of Viking culture), Sonya recognized the bigger drive: “A lot of the brands out there lean into that ‘dressed up as a Viking’ look,” says Sonya. Runestone promises the opposite; born as a way to embrace history through a modern lens with designs, symbols, and styles as “something anyone can wear and connect with, not just a costume,” says Sonya.

“Every design has a real story behind it—a god, a creature, a rune, and we care a lot about getting that story right,” Sonya continues. “We’re carrying forward the spirit of the Vikings more than the actual lifestyle, religion, or the more brutal parts of the history.”

Every week, Sonya receives emails, primarily from younger folks who are responding to the uptick in social media attention surrounding Viking culture. “They’re asking really specific questions,” she says, like inquiring about the gods—especially Odin, who is widely regarded as the god of wisdom and warfare—and requesting that Sonya point them toward reliable sources instead of pop culture tales.

For the curious travelers who make it to Norway, they have more opportunity than ever to engage with Viking heritage, from active opportunities like Viking Valley and shopping at Klesarven to passive participation at hotels.

In the northwestern Ålesund region, Storfjord Hotel was built in traditional Norwegian laft style with timber logs and turf roofs (the latter prioritized in Viking times for insulation). On Manshausen Island, located off the coast of northern Norway, the restaurant walls at the eponymous resort are covered with overlapping wooden scales built in the traditional Viking construction. Its groundskeeper team consists of two dozen sheep—an ancient Nordic breed that was kept during the Viking era.

“A hotel can become much more than a beautiful place to stay,” says Linda Gram Egede-Nissen, co-owner and CEO of interior design firm Gathe + Gram. “It can offer guests a subtle introduction to the culture and history of its surroundings.” In Trondheim, the northern city which served as the Viking capital of Norway many centuries ago, Gathe + Gram just completed the design blueprint for Eras, a boutique hotel where every room has its own distinctive name and story rooted in Viking history, mythology, or craftsmanship.

For this project, Gram Egede-Nissen was “particularly fascinated” by the “remarkable precision, complexity and beauty in the detailing” of historic jewelry from the Viking era. Her team translated the shapes, patterns, and proportions of spenne (buckles), skålspenne (ornamental brooches), and polyedrisk (beads) into architectural details and smaller design elements—decorative cushions, sculptural chandeliers, and wall art—throughout the interiors. “There is an incredible richness in the [Viking-era] jewelry—and many of these forms feel surprisingly relevant even today,” says Gram Egede-Nissen.

“To me, that is where heritage becomes truly relevant,” adds Gram Egede-Nissen. “Not when we preserve it as something untouchable, but when we allow it to inspire new ideas.”
